## File 1: `ai-context-plan.txt`

```text
MORCAFFEIN CRM — PROJECT PLAN & BUSINESS CONTEXT
(companion to ai-context-bundle.txt, which has the actual code — DELTA this time: only
files touched in the most recent session are listed there; everything else is unchanged
from the previous bundle. This file explains the WHY behind the system — the goal, the
decisions made along the way, and what's left.)

====================================================================
1. WHAT THIS PROJECT IS
====================================================================
A Coffee Shop Loyalty & Retention CRM ("Morcaffein") — a WinForms desktop app (.NET,
net10.0-windows) for the STAFF side of the business (baristas/managers at the counter),
backed by a real EF Core + SQL Server database (not just mocked long-term, though the UI
is currently wired to an in-memory mock service layer — see section 4).

The Staff UI has three pillars — ALL THREE ARE UI-COMPLETE against mock data:
  1. Transactions / POS — recording sales           -> DONE
  2. Customer management — search/register/history  -> DONE
  3. Feedback — logging + reviewing tickets         -> DONE (staff side only, see section 3)

Login/auth is explicitly OUT OF SCOPE for now. FrmLogin exists as a stub but is never
shown — Program.cs launches straight into FrmMain, and a placeholder employee session is
seeded in code (see section 4).

The project owner's next-step framing: connect everything to the real database, starting
with one service at a time. See section 8.

====================================================================
2. ARCHITECTURE / STACK DECISIONS
====================================================================
- WinForms, not WPF.
- Hand-rolled MVVM: no MVVM toolkit package. ObservableObject (INotifyPropertyChanged +
  SetProperty) and RelayCommand/RelayCommand<T> (ICommand) are small hand-written classes
  in Common/. Forms wire up ViewModels manually via code-behind event handlers — no
  Control.DataBindings, no XAML-style binding syntax.
- DDD-ish domain entities (CRM_Morcaffein.domain/entities): mostly private-set properties,
  mutated only through domain methods. Campaign is the one entity that still uses plain
  public get/set (not yet refactored).
- EF Core 10 with TenantCrmDbContext (IdentityDbContext-based), SQL Server provider. The
  connection string in CRM_Morcaffein.api/appsettings.json points to a REAL hosted SQL
  Server (db67068.public.databaseasp.net), not localhost. Migrations get generated/applied
  using CRM_Morcaffein.api as --startup-project.
- The DB is a MULTITENANT setup: one master DB tracks tenants, and the currently-connected
  tenant is "tenant A".
- "Card" table layout convention: every management tab (Customers, Feedback) uses the same
  boxed-table pattern — an outer padded panel, a white bordered card containing a header
  row (search box top-left, primary action button top-right) and the DataGridView below
  it. Transactions/POS deliberately breaks from this in its middle/right content since it's
  a different interaction model (a register, not a record browser), but still lives inside
  the same outer card convention for visual consistency.
- Left-side drawer convention: clicking a grid row opens a detail drawer on the LEFT of the
  card showing profile/ticket info. (Transactions/POS uses a left COLUMN for customer
  search instead of a drawer.)
- The outer card's `FixedSingle` border was REMOVED from Transactions this session — it
  doubled up with the Order box's own border on the right edge and read as a thick black
  seam. The Order/Payables/Log Sale boxes keep their own borders and the right column's
  padding insets them from the card edge.

====================================================================
3. KEY BUSINESS RULES
====================================================================
- POINT ADJUSTMENTS ARE A TWO-STEP APPROVAL WORKFLOW, NOT AN INSTANT EDIT:
    * A Manager (Employee.IsManager: Manager/Admin/SuperAdmin) can REQUEST a point
      adjustment for a customer (PointAdjustmentRequest, status "Pending"). Requests
      accept NEGATIVE amounts (deductions) as well as positive — the amount field is a
      NumericUpDown with a negative Minimum, and the domain handles the negative case.
    * Only an Admin (Employee.IsAdmin: Admin/SuperAdmin) can APPROVE or REJECT it.
      Approving actually applies the point change (via Customer.AdjustPoints) and writes
      a PointLedger row; rejecting just closes out the request with no balance change.
    * An employee can NEVER approve their own request.
    * This Staff/Manager app is explicitly NOT the admin console — the approve/reject UI
      exists in code but the placeholder session is seeded as Manager, so in THIS app
      you'll only ever see the "submit a request" half. Admin approval is a different,
      not-yet-built surface.
    * The customer's adjustment-requests list only shows PENDING requests.
- FEEDBACK — THIS APP IS LOG + VIEW ONLY:
    * Any staff member can log a feedback ticket against a customer.
    * The staff console does NOT resolve, dismiss, or award bonus points. Those are a
      MANAGER decision on how to address the feedback (reward or not) and belong on a
      future manager/admin surface. The decision panel that used to live in the Feedback
      drawer has been removed from this app entirely.
    * Staff-side flow: log a ticket → see it in the grid → click a row → see the review
      detail in the drawer (rating, category, status, date, notes). Nothing more.
- TRANSACTIONS/POS ALWAYS requires a real, identified Customer — there is no guest/walk-in
  checkout path in the UI. Picking a customer (via the ID/phone search box) is what starts
  a transaction; before that, the register displays but can't add to cart or check out.
  This is now permanent product policy: the program is designed for customers who are
  already loyalty members or want to register.
- SEARCH-AND-GO STARTS A FRESH TRANSACTION. If a search identifies a different customer
  while a cart has items in it, the app asks for confirmation ("Discard the in-progress
  order for X and start a new one for Y?") before throwing the cart away. Declining
  restores the search box to the currently-loaded customer's ID.
- PROMOS:
    * The promo control is a single BUTTON at the bottom of the left customer column. Its
      label shows the currently-applied promo ("Exam Week ▾") or "Select a Promo ▾". Click
      opens a menu of eligible promos; "Clear applied promo" appears at the top when one
      is active. There is no separate ComboBox — the button is both the state display and
      the action.
    * Applying a promo snapshots a CampaignRedeem row on the Order. Re-selecting the same
      promo is blocked at the UI level (Order.ApplyPromo has no duplicate guard of its
      own — that's a deferred domain fix, see section 7).
    * DISCOUNTS RE-EVALUATE WHEN THE CART CHANGES. Order.RecalculateTotals recomputes
      TotalDiscount by re-running each applied campaign's CalculateDiscount against the
      CURRENT SubTotal, not the snapshot taken at apply time. This is a domain change
      made this session; see section 6.
- Tiers (Regular/Silver/Gold) are labeled as plain text ONLY — no color-coding. Same for
  order/feedback status. The whole palette is brand-brown (#572400) tints/tones/shades
  plus plain white/grey neutrals only (see BrandPalette.cs).
- VAT and PWD/Senior discount on the POS Payables panel are DISPLAY-ONLY placeholders:
  VAT is shown as an informational 12%-of-total breakdown (assumes VAT-inclusive pricing,
  PH-receipt style) and does NOT change what's charged; PWD/Senior Disc. is a static
  ₱0.00 line with no input wired up yet.
- Guest/walk-in orders: the Order entity's constructor requires a positive CustomerId.
  The mock layer has a hidden MockDataStore.WalkInCustomer but the POS UI doesn't
  exercise it. With the "every sale needs a real customer" policy now settled, this is
  no longer a known limitation — it's just dead code that can be removed when the mock
  layer is replaced.

====================================================================
4. WHAT'S MOCKED VS REAL RIGHT NOW
====================================================================
- The domain entities, DbContext, and migrations are REAL and applied to the actual
  remote SQL Server database.
- The UI currently talks ONLY to an in-memory mock service layer (Services/Mock/*, all
  sharing one MockDataStore singleton via ServiceRegistry). This is deliberate — build
  the UI against mocks first, don't touch the real API/HTTPS layer yet. Section 8's
  "connect everything to the database" plan replaces this, one service at a time.
- ServiceRegistry.PlaceholderStaffAccount stands in for "whoever is logged in" until
  FrmLogin/real auth exists. Seeded as the Manager employee (Miguel Santos) specifically
  so the point-adjustment REQUEST flow is testable without an admin login, while
  approve/reject stays hidden.
- When real EF-backed services are ready: swap the right-hand side of each property in
  ServiceRegistry.cs and delete the Mock* classes plus Common/PrivateSetterAccessor.cs
  (a reflection shim only the mocks need).

====================================================================
5. UI DECISIONS — SHELL / CUSTOMERS / FEEDBACK
====================================================================
- Sidebar lives on the RIGHT. Distinct tone (Tint85) from page background (Tint95) and
  white card surfaces, footer a step darker (Tint75).
- A thin top bar spans the full width above the sidebar (brand mark + "Morcaffein" +
  active tab name), 60px tall. Transactions/POS does NOT get a second banner of its own.
- No account-switcher control — the logged-in staff name/role in the sidebar footer is a
  plain read-only Label, not a ComboBox.
- Table headers use Tint50 with dark text; selected-row highlight uses Tint90. Column-
  header click-to-sort doesn't flash the default system blue.
- Disabled buttons visibly grey out (BrandPalette.ButtonDisabledFill/Text via
  Theme/ButtonStyler.cs's TrackEnabledState helper).
- Star ratings (Feedback logging) are hollow (☆) when unfilled, solid brand-colored (★)
  up to the hovered/clicked count.
- Onboarding a new customer is a 2-step modal (Details -> Confirm) with a Back button.
- Log Feedback modal is also 2-step (pick customer via its own search -> rating/category/
  notes), with Cancel only on step 1, replaced by Back on step 2.
- The Feedback ticket drawer's review content is boxed into its own bordered card.
- Order History (Customers drawer) has NO Status column — every row is a completed sale.
- FEEDBACK DRAWER IS NOW REVIEW-ONLY. The decision panel (bonus points / resolution notes
  / Resolve & Award / Dismiss) that used to sit below the review box has been removed.
  Staff log and view; managers decide elsewhere.
- FEEDBACK / CUSTOMERS DRAWER GROUPING: the Feedback drawer boxes its review content;
  the Customers drawer boxes the profile block (name/tier/points/contact) in its own
  bordered card, matching that pattern. The three sub-grids below (Order History, Ledger,
  Adjustment Requests) remain loose header+grid pairs, not individually boxed.

====================================================================
6. TRANSACTIONS/POS — DESIGN
====================================================================
The owner sketched a low-fi wireframe (search bar, customer profile, drink cards with
S/M/L/XL size buttons, an Order box, a Payables box, "Log Sale"). Final layout
(Views/Controls/TransactionView.cs):

- ONE boxed card containing three regions side by side plus nothing outside it — no
  second top banner. Customer info lives inline in the left column.
- LEFT COLUMN (260px): a single search box that looks up ONLY by Customer ID or contact
  number. The matched customer's profile (name, tier, points, contact) appears below the
  search box once found. At the bottom of the column: the promo button (see section 3).
- MIDDLE: "Drinks" header + a "Sort by Category" ComboBox + a drink-name search box, then
  a wrapping FlowLayoutPanel of ProductCardControl cards. Each card shows S/M/L/XL
  quick-add buttons (positional labels by index, not derived from each product's actual
  SizeName text). Tapping one adds that size, qty 1, no modifiers, to the cart. Clicking
  the card body opens FrmItemCustomizer for modifiers / a different quantity.
- RIGHT COLUMN (380px): three bordered boxes stacked:
    * "Order" box (Fill, scrolls) listing CartLineControl rows.
    * "Payables" box (Bottom) with Subtotal / Discount / VAT (12%, display-only) /
      PWD-Senior Disc. (static ₱0.00 placeholder) / Total.
    * "Log Sale" box (Bottom) with a full-width Log Sale button.
  The column has 10px padding so all three boxes are inset uniformly from the card edge.

- CART LINE LAYOUT (Views/Controls/CartLineControl.cs):
    * Row is 44px. Left-to-right: name (fills, ellipsized single-line), price (76px,
      right-aligned ₱SubTotal), stepper cluster (94px: −, 1x, +), 10px gap, ✕ (28px).
    * The name label is height-constrained to a single line so AutoEllipsis fires instead
      of wrapping to two lines.
    * The stepper and ✕ are inside a shared rightCluster panel, with the gap between them
      being real empty space inside that panel — not a Margin between docked siblings
      (WinForms packs those flush and honors margins inconsistently).
    * Children are absolutely positioned in LayoutChildren(), called from OnResize and
      OnHandleCreated. Both children of the FlowLayoutPanel stepper carry
      Margin = new Padding(0) — FlowLayoutPanel's default 3px-per-side margin was
      squeezing the trailing + button out of the 94px stepper.
    * The ✕ is a Label, not a Button — WinForms FlatStyle buttons enforce a minimum width
      larger than 28px, which visually overlapped the +.

- GOTCHA WORTH REMEMBERING: never set Dock on a direct child of a FlowLayoutPanel — the
  panel positions children itself and Dock fights it. This was the original "cart lines
  don't render at all" bug.

- Seeded promos: Birthday Treat (20% off, birthday-only), Gold Member Perk (₱50 off,
  Gold tier + ₱200 min), We Miss You (15% off, inactive customers), and Exam Week
  (10% off, all tiers, no minimum, 50 redemptions) — the last one exists specifically so
  "Select a Promo" is never empty in ad-hoc testing.

====================================================================
7. PENDING / KNOWN GAPS
====================================================================
- Real login (FrmLogin) is deferred — not a bug, just not in scope yet.
- A future admin console (or an admin-capable login) is the natural home for:
    * The approve/reject side of the point-adjustment workflow.
    * The resolve/dismiss/award-bonus side of feedback handling (removed from this app
      this session — see section 3).
- VAT/PWD-Senior discount on the POS are cosmetic placeholders. Turning them into real,
  functioning discount logic is unassigned future work.
- Order.ApplyPromo has no duplicate guard at the domain level; the UI blocks re-selecting
  the same promo on one order, but the domain permits it. A domain-level guard is the
  proper fix and is deferred to the DB-connection workstream.
- The wireframe's sidebar sketch showed a standalone "Registration" nav item separate from
  Transactions/Customers/Feedback; this was NOT added.
- MENU REVISION (deferred, owner's next plan): the product catalog should become
  beverages only (hot & cold), with a base pricing scheme of Regular ₱30 / Large ₱40 /
  XL ₱50 and the modifiers ("additionals") adjusted to match. This is a content/data
  change to MockDataStore.SeedProducts / SeedModifiers and possibly the ProductCategory
  naming ("Espresso"/"Cold Brew" → "Hot"/"Cold"). Not scoped yet — waiting on the owner
  to detail it.
- SwitchCustomer (relink-the-existing-order) on TransactionViewModel is now unused by the
  POS flow — search-and-Go starts a fresh VM/Order instead. Left in place since the Quick
  Register relink flow may want it later; harmless if never called.

====================================================================
8. ACTIVE NEXT PLANS
====================================================================
Two workstreams, in order:

A) MENU REVISION (immediate next, per owner)
   - Beverages only (hot & cold categories).
   - Baseline size pricing: Regular ₱30 / Large ₱40 / XL ₱50.
   - "Additionals" (modifiers) re-priced to match.
   - Touches MockDataStore seed data and probably the category naming. Details to be
     documented by the owner before implementation.

B) CONNECT EVERYTHING TO THE REAL DATABASE (replace the mock service layer)
   - Write real EF-Core-backed implementations of each I*Service interface, one service
     at a time (starting with one — pattern reference to be established on the first).
   - ServiceRegistry.cs is the ONLY place that should need to change to wire in the real
     implementations.
   - PrivateSetterAccessor becomes dead code once the swap is done — delete with the
     Mock* classes.
   - ServiceRegistry.PlaceholderStaffAccount needs a real equivalent once there's a real
     Employees table to query.
   - Multitenant consideration: the master DB tracks tenants; the current connection
     string targets tenant A. Decide how tenant resolution works once real services
     exist (baked into the connection string vs. resolved per-session).
   - The connection string already points at a live, real, shared database — changes here
     are NOT sandboxed like the mock layer was. Be careful with anything that seeds or
     deletes data.
```

```text
    /// <summary>
    /// Non-persisted back-reference to the campaign this redemption was created for. EF Core
    /// populates Campaign automatically when loading from the database; this ensures the
    /// reference is also set at apply time (mock path), so RecalculateTotals can re-evaluate
    /// the discount against the current SubTotal instead of using a frozen snapshot.

===== FILE: CRM_Morcaffein.domain/entities/Order.cs =====
[only ApplyPromo and RecalculateTotals changed; the rest of the file is unchanged.
 Replace those two methods with:]

    public void ApplyPromo(Campaign campaign)
    {
        EnsureOrderIsPending();
        if (campaign is null) throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(campaign));

        decimal discount = campaign.CalculateDiscount(SubTotal);
        var redeem = new CampaignRedeem(campaign.CampaignId, OrderId, discount);
        redeem.AttachCampaign(campaign);   // so RecalculateTotals can re-evaluate later
        CampaignRedeems.Add(redeem);
        RecalculateTotals();
    }

    public void RemovePromo(Campaign campaign)
    {
        if (campaign == null) throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(campaign));

        EnsureOrderIsPending();

        var redeem = CampaignRedeems.FirstOrDefault(r => r.CampaignId == campaign.CampaignId);
        if (redeem is null)
            return;

        CampaignRedeems.Remove(redeem);
        RecalculateTotals();
    }

    public void RecalculateTotals()
    {
        SubTotal = OrderItems.Sum(item => item.SubTotal);

        // Re-evaluate each applied campaign against the CURRENT SubTotal rather than using
        // the snapshot taken at apply time — otherwise a percentage promo applied to a ₱100
        // cart stays frozen at its ₱10 discount even after the cart grows to ₱200.
        // CampaignRedeem carries the Campaign reference for exactly this reason (EF populates
        // it on load; ApplyPromo attaches it at creation).
        TotalDiscount = CampaignRedeems.Sum(redeem =>
        {
            if (redeem.Campaign is null)
                return redeem.DiscountUsed;   // fall back to snapshot if nav isn't loaded

            var freshDiscount = redeem.Campaign.CalculateDiscount(SubTotal);
            redeem.UpdateDiscountUsed(freshDiscount);
            return freshDiscount;
        });

        TotalAmount = Math.Max(0m, SubTotal - TotalDiscount);
    }

===== FILE: CRM_Morcaffein/Services/IOrderService.cs =====
[add this method to the interface, after ApplyPromo:]

    /// <summary>Wraps order.RemovePromo(campaign) — the counterpart to ApplyPromo.</summary>

===== FILE: CRM_Morcaffein/Services/Mock/MockOrderService.cs =====
[add this method after ApplyPromo:]

    public Order RemovePromo(Order order, Campaign campaign)
    {
        order.RemovePromo(campaign); // domain method recalculates totals itself
```

Good — pure discussion, no code. Let me lay out the actual decision points, because "connect to the DB" hides about six separate architectural calls, and getting them settled now saves re-doing them later.

---

## The core question: DTOs or entities directly?

**Short answer: no DTOs on the wire, but yes to some shape around reads.**

Here's the reasoning.

**Argument against DTOs everywhere:**

- The domain entities are already the right shape for the UI. `Customer` has `Tier`, `PointsBalance`, `FullName` as computed properties; `Order` has `SubTotal`/`TotalDiscount`/`TotalAmount`; `Feedback` has `TicketId`/`Rating`/`Status`. The ViewModels bind directly to these today (via `BindingList<Customer>`, `BindingList<Order>`, etc.).
- Introducing DTOs means every service method has to map entity → DTO on read and DTO → entity on write, and every ViewModel changes to bind to the DTO shape. That's a large mechanical refactor for zero behavior change.
- EF Core already materializes entities efficiently. The usual argument for DTOs (avoid over-fetching, decouple the wire shape) doesn't apply here — the "wire" is an in-process method call to an EF `DbContext`, not a network hop.

**Argument for DTOs in specific places:**

- **Read-side projections for grids.** `GetAll()` returning full `Customer` entities loads every column including unused ones. On a shop's real DB with thousands of customers, that's wasteful. A `CustomerSummary` DTO with just `CustomerId`, `FullName`, `ContactNumber`, `PointsBalance`, `Tier`, `LastVisitDate` is what the Customers grid actually needs.
- **Anything that crosses a session/transaction boundary.** If a `DbContext` is scoped per-operation, returning entities that are then bound to a `BindingList` in the ViewModel means the entities become detached — lazy-loaded nav properties (`Customer.Feedbacks`, `Order.OrderItems`) will throw when the grid tries to read them after the context is disposed. That's the classic "works in dev, throws in production" EF trap.

**My recommendation:** **entities directly, with `DbContext` scoped to the app's lifetime for the mock-replacement phase.** Not per-operation. That is:

- One `TenantCrmDbContext` instance lives as long as the app process, same as `MockDataStore` does today.
- Services take it via constructor injection, same as they take `MockDataStore` today.
- `ServiceRegistry` owns the instance (or a small factory if you want per-tenant later).
- Nav properties work because the context is never disposed mid-session.
- `BindingList<Customer>` keeps binding to the real entities with no DTO mapping.

This is not the EF best practice for web apps (short-lived contexts per request), but it's the correct pattern for a **long-running desktop app** that keeps entities alive in-memory and binds them to controls. The alternative — scoped contexts — forces DTOs everywhere, because the entities can't outlive the context.

**Where DTOs still make sense (later, not now):** if you later split the services into an actual API layer (the `CRM_Morcaffein.api` project suggests you might), DTOs become the boundary at that API edge, not at the ViewModel edge. That's a separate decision.

---

## The bigger decisions to settle

**1. Context lifetime.**
Already covered above: **app-lifetime singleton context**, not per-operation. It matches what the mocks do, avoids the detached-entity problem, and keeps `BindingList<T>` binding to real entities working. If you ever need to refresh from the DB, call `context.Entry(x).Reload()` rather than re-fetching.

**2. Save timing.**
Currently, mocks mutate in-memory and the state "sticks" immediately. With EF, every mutation needs a `SaveChanges()` at some point. Two patterns:

- **Immediate save:** every `AddItem`, `RemoveItem`, `CompleteOrder`, etc. calls `SaveChanges()` right after mutating. Simple. But a POS order being built up over several minutes would persist partial state to the DB after every item — if the app crashes mid-sale, the DB has a half-finished Pending order.
- **Deferred save:** mutations accumulate on the tracked entity, and `SaveChanges()` is called at defined commit points (after `CompleteOrder`, after `Register`, after `RequestAdjustment`). The order stays in-memory until the sale is finalized, then one transaction writes everything.

**My recommendation: deferred save.** It matches the domain better (an order isn't real until `CompleteOrder`), avoids partial-sale garbage, and makes `RemoveItem` a pure in-memory operation. Every service method that *should* persist calls `SaveChanges()`; ones that are mid-transaction don't.

The nuance: `Customer.AddPoints` is called inside `Order.CompleteOrder`. If the domain call is "mutate the entity," then `CompleteOrder`'s service method is the commit point — one `SaveChanges()` covers the order, the items, the campaign redeems, the points ledger row, and the customer's balance in one transaction. That's actually cleaner than the mock.

**3. Identity assignment.**
The mocks fake IDs via `PrivateSetterAccessor` (`NextCustomerId()`, `NextOrderId()`, etc.). EF assigns them on `SaveChanges()` from SQL Server identity columns. This means:

- Every place the mock does `customer.CustomerId = NextCustomerId()` becomes "do nothing — EF assigns it."
- Every `OrderItem` constructor that currently reads `order.OrderId` gets the real value only after `SaveChanges()`. **But `OrderItem`'s constructor snapshots `OrderId` from the parent — that snapshot would be 0 before save.** This needs a fix: either EF fixes up the FK on save (it does, if the relationship is configured and the nav is set), or `OrderItem` shouldn't snapshot `OrderId` in its constructor at all.
- The `Domain events / identity-after-save problem` is real. It's worth deciding upfront: do we let EF handle identity entirely (delete the ID-setting code from services), or do services pre-assign IDs? **Let EF handle it.** The `AddPoints` call inside `CompleteOrder` writes a `PointLedger` row with `CustomerId` — the customer already has an ID by that point (they're a saved customer), so that's fine. `OrderId` on the ledger row is nullable and gets filled by EF's relationship fixup.

**4. Navigation property loading.**
The mocks have everything in-memory, so `Customer.Orders`, `Order.OrderItems`, `Feedback.Customer` are always populated. With EF:

- **Eager loading:** `Include(c => c.Orders).ThenInclude(o => o.OrderItems)` etc. Explicit, but every query has to list what it wants.
- **Lazy loading:** needs `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Proxies` and virtual navs (which the entities already have). Automatic, but lazy loading is a footgun — a grid that touches `customer.Orders` triggers a query per row.
- **Explicit loading:** `context.Entry(customer).Collection(c => c.Orders).Load()`.

**My recommendation: eager loading in the specific read paths that need it** (`GetOrderHistory`, `GetLedger`, `GetForCustomer`), and **no lazy loading**. The entities already have `virtual` navs, so this is a per-query decision. The Customer grid itself (`GetAll`, `Search`) should *not* include orders — that's a per-row query trap.

**5. The `WalkInCustomer` question — resolved.**
We settled earlier that every sale needs a real customer. So `MockDataStore.WalkInCustomer` and any guest-order path become dead. The EF-backed `IOrderService.StartOrder(int customerId, ...)` should take a **non-nullable** `int customerId`. Confirm that's the intent and the interface signature changes to reflect it — probably worth doing now so the interface tells the truth.

**6. Transaction scope.**
Some operations are inherently multi-step. `CompleteOrder` writes:

- One `Order` row (status: Completed, totals, points earned)
- N `OrderItem` rows (already tracked as part of the order)
- M `OrderItemModifier` rows
- K `CampaignRedeem` rows
- One `PointLedger` row (via `Customer.AddPoints`)
- One `Customer` update (PointsBalance)

All of this needs to be atomic. `SaveChanges()` in EF Core wraps all tracked changes in a single transaction, so **one `SaveChanges()` call at the end of `CompleteOrder` handles it.** No explicit `BeginTransaction()` needed.

But if you have operations that span multiple `SaveChanges()` calls, you'd need an explicit transaction. **My recommendation: design every service method so it needs exactly one `SaveChanges()`.** If a method feels like it needs two, that's a sign the method is doing too much.

**7. Concurrency.**
Single-user desktop app, single-counter POS, no concurrent writers expected — **skip concurrency tokens for now.** EF's default optimistic concurrency (no token) means last-write-wins, which is fine for one app instance. If the multitenant DB has multiple devices hitting it simultaneously (which the `Device` entity suggests it might), you'd want `RowVersion` tokens. **Deferred until it's a real problem.**

**8. Error handling.**
The ViewModels currently catch `Exception` and call `OperationFailed` or set a status message. EF throws `DbUpdateException` on save failures, `InvalidOperationException` on invalid queries, etc. The ViewModels already catch broadly, so this mostly works — but you'll want to check that the messages are useful. **Deferred; not a first-pass concern.**

**9. Which service first.**
`ICustomerService` is the natural start: it's small (no complex writes, mostly reads + `Register`), it's used by three tabs (Transactions, Customers, Feedback's customer picker), and it doesn't touch the order lifecycle. Once it's done, you'll know exactly what the EF pattern looks like. `IProductCatalogService` is even simpler but less instructive (mostly reads). **Start with `ICustomerService`.**

**10. How to test the swap without breaking the app.**
Two strategies:

- **Parallel implementation, switch at the registry.** Write `EfCoreCustomerService`, leave `MockCustomerService` in place, and change `ServiceRegistry.Customers = new EfCoreCustomerService(...)`. If it breaks, flip back. Everything else is untouched because consumers depend only on `ICustomerService`. **This is the way.**
- **Big-bang replacement.** Replace all mocks at once, fix compile errors, hope for the best. **Avoid.**

**11. Real data vs. seed data.**
The DB already has migrations applied, which means tables exist. Do they have *rows*? If the tenant DB is empty, the UI will render blank grids — which might feel like "the swap broke it" when it's actually just empty. Decide: seed the DB with a few customers/products first (so the app has something to show), or accept empty grids and register everything through the UI.

**My recommendation: seed a small known dataset.** A few customers (Jasmine/Paolo/Liza as today), a few products, one employee — same as the mock seeds. Makes verification easy ("does the app show the same three customers as before?").

**12. `TenantCrmDbContext` construction.**
The connection string lives in `CRM_Morcaffein.api/appsettings.json`. The WinForms app doesn't read that file — it's the API project that holds the DI registration and design-time config. To use EF from the WinForms app, you need:

- The connection string accessible to the WinForms app (either a config file, a hardcoded constant in a sensible place, or an environment variable).
- A `DbContextOptionsBuilder` that configures `UseSqlServer(connectionString)`.
- A way to *create* the context once at startup and hand it to `ServiceRegistry`.

This is a real piece of plumbing that the plan file doesn't currently describe. It's the first thing to design when we start implementing.

---

## Where I'd land, as a summary

| Decision | Recommendation |
| --- | --- |
| DTOs | No — bind entities directly; context lives for the app's lifetime |
| Context lifetime | Singleton per app process |
| Save timing | Deferred — one `SaveChanges()` per logical operation (e.g. `CompleteOrder`) |
| Identity | Let EF assign; delete `PrivateSetterAccessor` usage from services |
| Nav loading | Eager, per read path; no lazy loading |
| Guest orders | Drop `WalkInCustomer`; `StartOrder` takes non-nullable `customerId` |
| Transactions | One `SaveChanges()` per service method; no explicit `BeginTransaction` unless needed |
| Concurrency | Skip for now |
| First service | `ICustomerService` |
| Migration strategy | Parallel implementation, switch at `ServiceRegistry` |
| Seed data | Seed a small known dataset first |
| Context plumbing | Design `DbContextOptionsBuilder` setup + connection-string source for the WinForms app first |

3. **DB state right now — is the tenant DB seeded with anything, or empty?** This determines whether the first EF-backed service will have data to show on day one, or whether we need to seed before testing.

## Three structural questions before I write anything

These matter because they change how many `Product` rows you end up with, and how the seed data is shaped:

**1. Hot vs Iced — separate products, or a modifier?**

For each matcha flavor, do you want:

- **(a) Two products:** "Matcha Latte (Hot)" and "Matcha Latte (Iced)" — simple to seed, but doubles the product list and splits sales reporting
- **(b) One product + a Hot/Iced modifier** — cleaner data model, one product per flavor, but the modifier adds ₱0 to price (it's just a state flag) and the staff has to actively pick

Same question for the chocolates. My recommendation is **(b)** — Hot/Iced is a temperature state, not a different product, and your schema already has a modifier system. But it changes the UI flow (staff taps the drink card → picks Hot/Iced → picks size).

**2. Size pricing — is ₱30/40/50 truly universal across everything?**

Matcha in the real world costs more than hot chocolate. If matcha Regular is ₱60 and hot chocolate Regular is ₱30, then size pricing isn't universal and each product needs its own size rows. If everything is ₱30/40/50 flat, we can simplify the schema (a shared price table, or just set every size row to the same values).

**3. Flavor variants — separate products, or a modifier?**

Strawberry Matcha, Vanilla Matcha, Honey Matcha — three products, or one "Matcha Latte" with a flavor modifier? You said "Matcha 1–14 should just be bundled," which I read as "don't give matcha its own nav section," not "collapse the flavors." But this is worth being explicit about because it's the biggest schema decision here.

If flavors are modifiers: 1 matcha product + flavor modifier × Hot/Iced modifier × size = a very tight product list, and the POS flow becomes "tap Matcha → pick flavor → pick temp → pick size."

If flavors are products: 10 matcha products (5 flavors × 2 temps), each with size rows.

**Your schema supports either.** The modifier route is cleaner data-wise but requires more taps per sale. The product route is more taps-free but bloats the product list.

## The Hot/Iced structural question — discussion only, no decision

You said: *"if my system UI so far can handle iced hot modifier and the database says so then go for it. but if not then I very much prefer the separate matcha latte hot and matcha latte cold pattern."*

**What the system can and can't do, honestly:**

**The database can absolutely handle it.** `ProductModifier` is a real table with `Name`, `Category`, `Price`, and `OrderItemModifier` snapshots it into order lines. A "Hot/Iced" modifier with `Price = 0` is fully supported by the schema. Nothing needs to change at the DB level.

**The UI can technically handle it, but it changes the flow.** Right now, tapping a drink card either:

- Quick-adds (S/M/L/XL button on the card → straight to cart), or
- Opens `FrmItemCustomizer` (card body click → pick size, pick modifiers, pick qty)

If Hot/Iced is a modifier, then **every drink with a temperature option can no longer use the quick-add buttons** — because the quick-add path skips the modifier screen. So either:

- The card's quick-add buttons would need a hot/iced choice built in (S-M-L on top, Hot/Iced underneath, doubling the button count), or
- All temp-optional drinks force the customizer modal, slowing down the POS

**That's the real tension** — and it's why you asked for "faster POS over more taps." A modifier-based Hot/Iced **actively slows down the POS** unless we redesign the card. A separate product per temp (Matcha Latte Hot / Matcha Latte Iced as two cards) keeps quick-add intact: tap the right card, tap a size, done. **Two taps, no modal.**

**So the honest answer to your question:**

- **Database says yes** to the modifier approach.
- **UI currently says no** — using a modifier would force the slower customizer path for every temp-optional drink, which is the opposite of what you want.
- **Therefore, your fallback preference ("separate Matcha Latte Hot / Matcha Latte Cold") is actually the right call** for the POS flow you want, **not just a fallback.**

**But you said don't finalize it, so I won't.** For "later," the actual question to discuss is:

> Do we want speed (separate products, one tap per drink) or data cleanliness (one product, modifier)? Speed is achievable both ways, but only if we redesign the drink card to include temp buttons — which is a UI change, not a schema change.

That's the real trade. Not "can the system do it," but "does the card get redesigned to support it, or do we split products." Worth having in the plan file as an open question, not a decision yet.

## Add-ons — let's talk

Here's what I need from you to shape this well. I'll frame it as questions because add-ons are genuinely a design space, and the answers change both the schema usage and the POS flow.

### The existing schema

`ProductModifier` has: `Name`, `Category`, `Price`. Each `OrderItem` snapshots selected modifiers via `OrderItemModifier` (name + price snapshot at time of sale). Categories are free-text labels — no behavior attached.

### The questions

**1. What add-on *types* do you want?**

Common cafe add-on types:

- **Milk swap** — Oat Milk, Almond Milk, Soy Milk (usually +₱20–40)
- **Extra shots** — Extra Espresso Shot (+₱30–40), Extra Matcha Scoop (+₱40–50)
- **Syrups** — Vanilla, Caramel, Hazelnut, Brown Sugar, Sea Salt, Ube (+₱15–25)
- **Toppings** — Whipped Cream, Cold Foam, Marshmallows, Cocoa Dust, Cinnamon (+₱15–30)
- **Prep** — Less Ice, Extra Ice, Hot/Cold (if you hadn't already decided to split temp as products), No Sugar
- **Size upgrade** — but that's already handled by ProductSize, so probably not here

Which of those do you want as a first pass? You don't have to say "all" — some cafes skip milk swaps entirely if they only use one milk; some skip prep modifiers because staff just handle it verbally.

**2. Are add-ons universal, or restricted to certain drinks?**

The schema today doesn't model "this modifier only applies to this product." If you want "Extra Matcha Scoop" to only appear on matcha drinks, or "Extra Shot" only on coffees, that's a schema or logic change. Three options:

- **(a) Universal** — every add-on is available on every drink. Simplest. Staff/UI shows all add-ons on every drink's customizer. Weird combinations possible (matcha + espresso shot), but staff can just not pick them.
- **(b) Free-for-all with sane defaults** — universal list, but the customizer visually groups them by category so staff scroll to the relevant group.
- **(c) Per-product restriction** — a product→modifier mapping. Cleanest UX, but adds a join table or a product-tag system and more seed data.

My read for a fast POS: **(b)**. But if you want the database to actually forbid nonsensical combos, that's (c).

**3. Free add-ons or all priced?**

Some modifiers should be ₱0 — Less Ice, No Sugar, Extra Ice are all free prep notes. Others (milk swap, extra shots, syrups) cost. The schema supports both (Price can be 0). Do you want to include free prep modifiers, and if so, is the UI going to make that obvious (e.g. show "Free" instead of "+₱0")?

**4. Do add-ons have size-dependent pricing?**

E.g., Oat Milk +₱20 on Regular, +₱30 on Large. The schema does **not** support this today — each `ProductModifier` has a single price. If you want size-tiered add-on pricing, that's a schema change (`ProductModifierPrice` per size, or price-as-a-modifier-of-modifier). My guess is you want flat pricing and this isn't a concern, but worth confirming.

**5. Naming/grouping — do you want `Category` to be meaningful?**

Right now `Category` is just a display grouping label ("Milk", "Syrup", "Topping"). If it stays that way, fine. If you want it to gate anything (e.g., UI ordering, "only show Milk group on coffees"), it becomes more than a label. My recommendation: **keep it as a display grouping only**, non-behavioral.

---

## Two observations worth flagging before you answer

**Observation 1: "Less Ice" is currently a modifier with a ₱0 price.** If you're going to split drinks into (Hot)/(Cold) products, "Hot/Iced" itself is no longer a modifier — but "Less Ice" still makes sense as a cold-only modifier. However, "Less Ice" on a *Hot* Americano makes no sense. That's the per-product restriction problem (question 2) — if you go universal, the UI has to trust staff to not pick "Less Ice" on a hot drink. If you go per-product, cold drinks get cold modifiers and hot drinks get hot modifiers.

**Observation 2: Sugar level and milk swap are the two add-ons most cafes use that aren't in your schema at all today.** Not a schema problem — they'd just be more `ProductModifier` rows. But worth naming so you decide intentionally rather than inheriting the default list (Extra Shot, Oat Milk, Almond Milk, Extra Syrup Pump, Whipped Cream, Less Ice) that shipped with the mock.

```text
file documents the menu as designed — both the drink list and the
modifier/add-on list — so the seed data and any future re-seeding
have a single source of truth.)
====================================================================

STATUS
====================================================================
Design LOCKED. Not yet implemented in code (still on the mock
product catalog as of this writing). Implementation is the "menu
revision" workstream described in ai-context-plan.txt section 8.

This spec supersedes the seeded products and modifiers currently in
MockDataStore.SeedProducts() and SeedModifiers(). When the menu
revision is implemented, replace those seeds entirely with what's
below.

====================================================================
SCOPE NOTES
====================================================================
- No inventory tracking. This system is POS-only — it records sales
  and awards loyalty points; it does not decrement stock, warn about
  low inventory, or track ingredient quantities. "In stock / out of
  stock" states do not exist as a concept.
- No coffee drinks were in the original seed data; this spec adds
  them. The shop's identity is matcha-forward, but the menu
  includes a full coffee and iced-coffee lineup for breadth.
- Hot/Iced is expressed as SEPARATE PRODUCTS, not as a modifier.
  Each temp-optional drink exists as two product rows labelled with
  a (Hot) or (Cold) suffix. This is a deliberate choice to keep the
  POS fast — tapping a drink card then a size adds directly to the
  cart without any modal, and no Hot/Iced modifier has to be picked
  mid-sale.
- Size pricing is UNIFORM across the entire menu: Regular ₱39,
  Large ₱49, XL ₱59. Every drink has all three sizes, matcha
  included. There is no per-category or per-product size exception.
- Add-ons are UNIVERSAL: every modifier is available on every
  drink. Nothing is restricted per-product or per-category at the
  data level. The UI groups modifiers by category for scannability
  (Milk Swaps / Extra Shots / Syrups / Toppings / Prep) but this
  grouping is DISPLAY-ONLY — it gates nothing.
- Add-on pricing is FLAT per add-on. No size-tiered pricing. ₱0 is
  a valid price for prep modifiers.
- There are NO default modifiers. Every add-on is opt-in; the order
  line only records what the staff explicitly selects.

  Sea Salt Syrup        +₱10

--- TOPPINGS ---

====================================================================
DELIBERATE DECISIONS — WHY
====================================================================
Captured so future readers understand these aren't defaults that
just happened; they're choices.

1. Hot/Iced as products, not a modifier.
   Rationale: POS speed. A "Hot/Iced" modifier would force every
   temp-optional drink through the item-customizer modal (because
   the quick-add size buttons on the drink card can't express a
   modifier choice), adding a step to the most common sale. Two
   products per temp keeps the quick-add flow intact: tap card, tap
   size, done.

2. Uniform size pricing.
   Rationale: simplicity. Per-category or per-product pricing
   schemes add branching to the UI (the drink card has to know
   whether to show 2 or 3 size buttons) and to the seed data. A
   single 3-tier price applied uniformly removes both branches.
   Business accepts that matcha costs more to produce than it's
   priced at, as a menu-simplification trade.

3. Universal modifiers.
   Rationale: staff discretion over system enforcement. A matcha
   drink with an "Extra Espresso Shot" is unusual but not illegal —
   the shop would rather let staff make that call than build and
   maintain a product→modifier mapping. The category grouping in
   the UI makes the relevant modifiers easy to find, so nonsensical
   combinations are unlikely to be picked by mistake.

4. Flat modifier pricing.
   Rationale: menu legibility. Size-tiered modifier pricing (Oat
   Milk +₱20 on Regular, +₱30 on Large) multiplies the modifier
   table's size and adds cognitive load at the register. Flat
   pricing means "Oat Milk is +₱20" is true for every drink, every
   size.

5. ₱0 prep modifiers.
   Rationale: the POS should record how a drink was made, not just
   what it cost. "Less Ice" and "Half Sugar" being ₱0 doesn't make
   them worthless data — they're part of the order record and
   matter if a customer disputes what they received.

6. No inventory tracking.
   Rationale: this is a POS + loyalty system, not a stock system.
   Ingredient consumption, low-stock warnings, and reorder points
   are out of scope. Products are either on the menu or they aren't;
   "is this drink currently available?" is not modeled.

These are known but deliberately left for later:
```

Short answer: **partially.** Three of the five are satisfied; two have gaps. Let me walk through each honestly against what's actually in the code.

## What you asked, item by item

### 1. Who made the transaction — ✅ YES

`Order.CreatedBy` (int) is set in the constructor from `createdByEmployeeId`, which flows from `EmployeeSession.Current.EmployeeId` → `TransactionViewModel` constructor → `_orderService.StartOrder(customerId, createdByEmployeeId)`. Every order records who rang it up. `Order.Employee` nav points at the `Employee`. `EmployeeSession` is a real single-source-of-truth for "who is logged in" — it's just that login itself isn't wired up yet (placeholder session).

### 2. Who requested — ⚠️ PARTIAL

Depends on what "requested" refers to:

- **For a sale:** the creator of the order is the requester. ✅ Covered by #1.
- **For a point adjustment:** `PointAdjustmentRequest.RequestedBy` (int) + `Requester` nav. ✅ Covered. `MockPointAdjustmentService.RequestAdjustment` takes `requestedByEmployeeId`, and `CustomerProfileViewModel.SubmitRequest` passes `EmployeeSession.Current.EmployeeId`. So the requester is recorded.
- **For feedback:** `Feedback.LoggedBy` (int) + `LoggedByEmployee` nav. ✅ Covered.
- **For a campaign:** `Campaign.MadeBy` + `Campaign.ApprovedBy`. ✅ Covered (though campaigns aren't created through any UI in this app).

So "who requested" is covered **everywhere there's a "request" concept**. No gap.

### 3. When — ✅ YES

- `BaseEntity.CreatedAt` / `UpdatedAt` on every entity. Set at construction time (`DateTime.UtcNow`).
- `Order.OrderDate` (set in constructor).
- `PointAdjustmentRequest.RequestedAt` / `DecidedAt`.
- `PointLedger.Timestamp`.
- `Feedback.DateLogged`.
- `CampaignRedeem.RedeemDate`.

Every audit-relevant event has a timestamp. No gap.

### 4. Who validated — ⚠️ PARTIAL

- **Point adjustment:** ✅ `PointAdjustmentRequest.ApprovedBy` + `Approver` nav + `DecidedAt` + `DecisionNotes`. Fully modeled. The **approval half is UI-unreachable** in this app (placeholder session is a Manager, not Admin), but the data model and service layer support it.
- **Campaign:** `Campaign.ApprovedBy` + `Approver` nav exist. Not exercised by any UI.
- **Sale (order):** ❌ **no validator field.** `Order` has `CreatedBy` but no `ValidatedBy` or `ApprovedBy`. In a POS, "validated" typically means "the transaction completed" (`Status = "Completed"`) and "who rang it up" — which the creator covers. But if "validated" means "a manager signed off on a discount / void / refund / price override," that concept doesn't exist at all.
- **Feedback:** ❌ **no validator field on `Feedback`.** `Feedback.Status` moves from "Pending" to "Resolved" or "Dismissed," but there's no `ResolvedBy` / `DismissedBy` / `HandledBy` employee field and no `ResolvedAt`. If a manager later resolves a ticket on the admin surface, the domain would currently have nowhere to record *who* did it. That's a real gap.
- **Point ledger entries:** `PointLedger.PerformedBy` exists and is populated when a point adjustment is approved. ✅ For earned/redeemed ledger rows it's null (nothing to attribute).

So: **"who validated" is modelled for point adjustments and campaigns, absent for orders and feedback.**

### 5. How to validate — ⚠️ PARTIAL / mostly UI

"Validate" as a business concept:

- **Point adjustment:** ✅ The full two-step flow exists — Manager requests, Admin approves, self-approval blocked. Domain, service, and (partial) UI all present. The approve/reject UI is unreachable in this app but exists in code.
- **Order completion:** the `CompleteOrder()` domain method is the implicit "validation" — it moves the order from Pending to Completed, computes points, and locks further edits. There's no separate "manager validates the sale" step, and there shouldn't be for a normal POS sale.
- **Feedback resolution:** was just **removed from this app** this session (by your request — the decision belongs to managers). The service methods (`ResolveFeedback`, `DismissFeedback`) still exist; the UI is gone. The eventual manager/admin surface would call those.
- **Void / refund / discount override:** ❌ **does not exist.** No concept of voiding a completed order, refunding a sale, or applying a manager-approved discount override. If a staff member rings up the wrong thing, there's no correction path. This is a real gap for a POS, but it may be out of scope for the current phase.

## Two things I'd flag as decisions, not bugs

**A. Does "validated" apply to orders at all?**

In a single-operator POS, the person who rang up the sale *is* the validator — there's nothing to approve. `Order.Status = "Completed"` is the state transition; `CreatedBy` is the attributed employee. If that's your definition, **orders are satisfied** and no field is missing.

But if "validated" means "a second person confirmed something" — a void, a refund, a discount override, a large transaction — then nothing in the system supports that today. That's a real feature gap and would need new fields (`Order.VoidedBy`, `Order.VoidReason`, or a separate `OrderValidation` entity) plus UI.

**Which does your business actually need?** That's the crux. If it's the first, you're done. If it's the second, we scope a void/correction workflow.

**B. The Feedback validator gap is a real one, and I'd fix it before building the admin surface.**

When the future manager console resolves a feedback ticket, `Feedback` currently has:

- `Status` (Pending → Resolved / Dismissed) ✅
- `DateLogged` ✅
- `LoggedBy` (who logged the *ticket*) ✅
- **no `ResolvedBy` / `ResolvedAt` / `DismissedBy`** ❌

`MarkAsResolved(string)` appends resolution notes to `StaffNotes` with a timestamp — but no employee ID. `Dismiss()` records nothing at all. So the moment a manager acts on a ticket, the system can't say **who** decided, or **when** (well, the timestamp is in the appended text, but not structured).

That's a straightforward domain fix: add `ResolvedBy` (int?), `ResolvedAt` (DateTime?), and change `Dismiss()` to take a `dismissedBy` and timestamp. Small, self-contained, deferred to whenever the admin surface is built — but I'd flag it now so it doesn't get forgotten.

---

## Where this leaves you

The system **satisfies the audit trail for everything it currently does** — orders, point-adjustment requests, feedback logging, point ledger entries all have who/when attribution. Two gaps are **forward-looking**:

1. **Feedback resolution attribution** — needed once the admin/manager surface exists.
2. **Void / refund / correction** — needed if the business ever needs to reverse a sale.

Neither is a "the system is broken" problem — both are "the system doesn't do this yet." Whether they're *required for the current phase* depends on your answer to question A: does "validate" apply to a plain sale, or only to exceptions?

**My question back to you:** when you say "who validated," were you asking about *every sale* (in which case the current model is fine — creator is validator), or about *exceptions* (voids, refunds, overrides) that need a separate approver? That determines whether there's actual work to do here or whether the requirements are already met.

## Part 1: "Who requested = who was the customer"

Under that reading, everything is covered:

- **Order** → `Order.CustomerId` + `Customer` nav. The customer who "requested" the sale is recorded on every order.
- **Feedback** → `Feedback.CustomerId` + `Customer` nav. The customer the ticket is about is recorded.
- **Point adjustment** → `PointAdjustmentRequest.CustomerId` + `Customer` nav. The customer whose points are being adjusted is recorded.
- **Point ledger** → `PointLedger.CustomerId` + `Customer` nav. Every points movement is attributed to a customer.

So "who requested" = customer → ✅ fully satisfied everywhere. No gap.

---

## Part 2: The defense question — "is the points adjustment system the void-a-sale mechanism?"

**No, and here's why you should say that clearly.**

They're two different things, and conflating them in a defense will get you picked apart:

**The points adjustment system:**

- Records a *change to a loyalty point balance* — +/- N points, with a reason, on a specific customer.
- Doesn't touch sales, orders, revenue, or receipts.
- Approval is a *loyalty-integrity* control: only an admin can decide "yes, this customer really deserves 200 bonus points."
- Its scope is points.

**Voiding a sale would need to:**

- Reverse an `Order` — change its status from `Completed` to `Voided`, or create a reversal record.
- Reverse the *points earned* on that order — which, coincidentally, could go through the points adjustment system as a negative adjustment.
- Reverse the *revenue*, which the CRM doesn't track at all (it's a POS + loyalty system, not an accounting system).
- Attribute *who* voided it and *why* — an audit trail separate from the points trail.

**Where they overlap:** the *points side* of a void — "this customer earned 50 points on a sale that's now being reversed, so deduct 50" — *could* be expressed as a point adjustment. `PointAdjustmentRequest` with `PointsChange = -50`, reason "Voided order #1234." That's actually a clean fit and might be exactly what you're thinking.

**Where they don't overlap:** the *order side*. Even if you deduct the points via an adjustment request, the original `Order` row still says `Status = "Completed"`, still shows in the customer's order history, still counted toward revenue in any report. The points adjustment doesn't touch the order. So the sale is only *half*-voided.

**The honest defense framing:**

> "Voiding a sale is out of scope for this phase. The points-earned component of a void can be handled through the existing point adjustment workflow as a negative adjustment with a reason — that part is covered. But the order record itself has no void/refund status, and adding one is future work if the business needs it. The CRM's job is loyalty points and customer records; sales-record correction is a POS/accounting concern."

That's defensible. What would be *indefensible* is claiming "voiding is fully handled by the point adjustment system," because a reader can trivially point at `Order.Status` and see there's no voided state.

---

## Part 3: "The validation points in the UI — do they exist in the database?"

This is the important question, and the answer is **mixed**. Let me go through each validation point that exists in the UI and check what's actually persisted.

### Point adjustment — ✅ Fully in the database

**UI:** Manager submits a request from `CustomerProfileViewModel.SubmitRequest`; admin approve/reject UI exists (unreachable in this app, but coded).

**Database:** `PointAdjustmentRequest` entity has:

- `RequestedBy` + `Requester` nav → who asked
- `RequestedAt` → when asked
- `ApprovedBy` + `Approver` nav → who decided
- `DecidedAt` → when decided
- `DecisionNotes` → why
- `Status` ("Pending" / "Approved" / "Rejected")

All persisted columns. **Fully modeled.** The only caveat: the admin side isn't reachable from this app, so nothing ever *writes* an Approved/Rejected row in practice — but the schema supports it.

### Feedback — ⚠️ Partially in the database

**UI:** previously had Resolve/Dismiss. **You removed that this session** — this app now only logs and views. The decision-making UI is slated for a future manager surface.

**Database:** `Feedback` has:

- `LoggedBy` + `LoggedByEmployee` nav → who logged the ticket ✅
- `DateLogged` → when logged ✅
- `Status` ("Pending" / "Resolved" / "Dismissed") ✅
- `MarkAsResolved(string)` → appends resolution notes to `StaffNotes` with a timestamp **in text** ⚠️
- `Dismiss()` → changes status, records **nothing** ❌

**Missing:**

- No `ResolvedBy` / `DismissedBy` employee field
- No `ResolvedAt` / `DecidedAt` structured timestamp
- No `ResolutionNotes` as its own column (currently concatenated into `StaffNotes` as free text with a `[timestamp]` prefix)

So the **feedback decision is not properly recorded in the database** — status yes, attribution no. If a manager resolves a ticket on the future admin surface, the DB can't say who did it or when, except as a text blob in `StaffNotes` that has to be parsed.

**This is a real gap.** Small fix, but it's a gap. Worth flagging in a defense as "known, planned for the admin-surface phase."

### Order completion — ⚠️ No separate validation, but the "creator is the operator" model covers it

**UI:** the "Log Sale" button triggers `CompleteSaleCommand`.

**Database:** `Order.Status` ("Pending" → "Completed"), `Order.OrderDate`, `Order.PointsEarned`, `Order.CreatedBy`. The completion *is* the validation — there's no separate approver, and for a normal POS sale there shouldn't be. If a reader asks "who validated this sale?" the answer is "the same person who created it — `CreatedBy` — and the completion is the state transition."

That's defensible, provided your business doesn't need a second-person check on any sales.

### Point ledger — ✅ Fully in the database

`PointLedger` has `CustomerId`, `PointsChange`, `Type`, `Reason`, `OrderId` (nullable), `PerformedBy` (nullable, employee who performed/approved), `Timestamp`. Every points movement is attributed.

The `PerformedBy` field is populated for adjustments (via `Customer.AdjustPoints(..., performedByEmployeeId)`). For earned/redeemed rows tied to an order, it's null — but the `Order.CreatedBy` tells you who rang it, so it's recoverable through the join.

## What I'd tell you to say in the defense

1. **Customer attribution** is complete across every entity that has a customer. ✅
2. **Point adjustments** have full request/approve/reject audit trail in the database — requester, approver, timestamps, decision notes, self-approval prevention. ✅

4. **Orders** are attributed to their creator; completion is the validation. For a single-operator POS this is the correct model. If a second-person check on sales becomes a requirement, it's a future scope addition.
5. **Void/refund is out of scope.** The *points-reversal* half of a void could flow through the point adjustment system as a negative adjustment — that part is genuinely covered. But reversing the *order* itself is not modeled, and shouldn't be claimed as covered. Frame it as POS/accounting territory, not CRM territory.

## Design

**Fields to add to `Feedback`:**

```csharp
public int? ResolvedBy { get; private set; }              // nullable — only set on Resolved/Dismissed
public DateTime? ResolvedAt { get; private set; }         // nullable — only set on Resolved/Dismissed
public string? ResolutionNotes { get; private set; }      // nullable — separate column, was concatenated into StaffNotes
```

**Why these three:**

- `ResolvedBy` — employee ID who made the decision. Nullable because it's only meaningful once `Status != "Pending"`.
- `ResolvedAt` — structured timestamp for when the decision was made. Not free text.
- `ResolutionNotes` — the decision's notes should be a real column, not appended into `StaffNotes` as `\n\n[yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm] Resolved: ...`. Keeping it separate means the original customer-facing notes stay untouched, and the resolution reason is queryable.

**Fields to *not* add:**

- No separate `DismissedBy` / `DismissedAt`. Resolve and Dismiss are two possible *outcomes* of the same decision — one set of fields covers both. `Status` distinguishes them, and `ResolvedBy`/`ResolvedAt`/`ResolutionNotes` are populated regardless of which way the decision went. (Naming could be `DecidedBy`/`DecidedAt` to be neutral, but I'll stick with `Resolved*` to match the existing `Status` vocabulary where "Resolved" is one of the outcomes.)

**Nav property:**

```csharp
public virtual Employee? ResolvedByEmployee { get; protected set; }
```

Consistent with `LoggedByEmployee`.

**Method signature changes:**

```csharp
public void MarkAsResolved(int resolvedByEmployeeId, string resolutionNotes)
public void Dismiss(int dismissedByEmployeeId, string? reason = null)
```

Both now require the acting employee's ID. `MarkAsResolved` keeps requiring resolution notes (existing behavior). `Dismiss` takes an optional reason — dismissals don't always need justification, but we should have somewhere to put one if given.

**Domain invariants inside the methods:**

- `resolvedByEmployeeId > 0` (throws otherwise)
- `Status` must be `"Pending"` to decide (currently `MarkAsResolved` and `Dismiss` don't check this — meaning you could re-resolve an already-resolved ticket. Should guard against that.)
- Both set `ResolvedBy`, `ResolvedAt = DateTime.UtcNow`.

## 1. `CRM_Morcaffein.domain/entities/Feedback.cs` — full replacement

```csharp
using System;

namespace CRM_Morcaffein.domain.entities;

public class Feedback : BaseEntity
{
    public int TicketId { get; private set; }
    public int CustomerId { get; private set; }
    public int LoggedBy { get; private set; }
    public int Rating { get; private set; } // CSAT score 1 to 5
    public string Category { get; private set; } = string.Empty;
    public string StaffNotes { get; private set; } = string.Empty;
    public string Status { get; private set; } = "Pending"; // "Pending", "Resolved", "Dismissed"
    public DateTime DateLogged { get; private set; } = DateTime.UtcNow;

    // Decision attribution — populated only once Status leaves "Pending". One set of fields
    // covers both outcomes (Resolved and Dismissed); Status distinguishes them. Mirrors
    // PointAdjustmentRequest.DecidedBy/DecidedAt/DecisionNotes so the audit vocabulary is
    // consistent across the two approval-style workflows in the domain.
    public int? DecidedBy { get; private set; }
    public DateTime? DecidedAt { get; private set; }
    public string? DecisionNotes { get; private set; }

    public virtual Customer? Customer { get; protected set; }
    public virtual Employee? LoggedByEmployee { get; protected set; }
    public virtual Employee? DecidedByEmployee { get; protected set; }

    public Feedback() : base() { }

    public Feedback(int customerId, int loggedBy, int rating, string category, string staffNotes) : base()
    {
        if (customerId <= 0) throw new ArgumentException("Customer ID is required.");
        if (loggedBy <= 0) throw new ArgumentException("Employee ID is required.");

        SetRating(rating);
        CustomerId = customerId;
        LoggedBy = loggedBy;
        Category = category;
        StaffNotes = staffNotes;
    }

    public void SetRating(int rating)
    {
        if (rating < 1 || rating > 5)
            throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(rating), "Rating must be between 1 and 5 stars.");
        Rating = rating;
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// Closes the ticket as Resolved. Decision attribution is written to DecidedBy/DecidedAt,
    /// and the resolution notes to DecisionNotes — StaffNotes is left untouched (it's the
    /// logging-time customer-facing notes, not a decision log).
    /// </summary>
    public void MarkAsResolved(int resolvedByEmployeeId, string resolutionNotes)
    {
        EnsurePending();

        if (resolvedByEmployeeId <= 0)
            throw new ArgumentException("Resolving employee ID is required.");
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(resolutionNotes))
            throw new ArgumentException("Resolution notes are required.");

        Status = "Resolved";
        DecidedBy = resolvedByEmployeeId;
        DecidedAt = DateTime.UtcNow;
        DecisionNotes = resolutionNotes.Trim();
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// Closes the ticket as Dismissed. A reason is optional — dismissal is often "not
    /// actionable" with no explanation needed, unlike a point-adjustment rejection which
    /// is a decision against an explicit request.
    /// </summary>
    public void Dismiss(int dismissedByEmployeeId, string? reason = null)
    {
        EnsurePending();

        if (dismissedByEmployeeId <= 0)
            throw new ArgumentException("Dismissing employee ID is required.");

        Status = "Dismissed";
        DecidedBy = dismissedByEmployeeId;
        DecidedAt = DateTime.UtcNow;
        DecisionNotes = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(reason) ? null : reason.Trim();
    }

    private void EnsurePending()
    {
        if (!Status.Equals("Pending", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
            throw new InvalidOperationException($"This ticket has already been {Status}.");
    }
}
```

**What changed:**

- Added `DecidedBy`, `DecidedAt`, `DecisionNotes` (all nullable).
- Added `DecidedByEmployee` nav.
- `MarkAsResolved` now takes `resolvedByEmployeeId` and writes the new fields; no longer appends to `StaffNotes`.
- `Dismiss` now takes `dismissedByEmployeeId` and an optional `reason`; writes the new fields.
- Both call `EnsurePending()` — a decided ticket can't be re-decided.

```csharp
builder.Entity<Feedback>(entity =>

    entity.HasKey(f => f.TicketId);
    entity.Property(f => f.Category).HasMaxLength(100);
    entity.Property(f => f.Status).HasMaxLength(50);

    entity.HasOne(f => f.LoggedByEmployee)

          .HasForeignKey(f => f.LoggedBy)
          .OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Restrict);

    entity.HasOne(f => f.DecidedByEmployee)
          .WithMany()
          .HasForeignKey(f => f.DecidedBy)
          .OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Restrict);
});
```

## Your three questions

### 1. Who made the feedback? → ✅ `LoggedBy`

The employee who logged the ticket. Set in the constructor (`Feedback(customerId, loggedBy, ...)`), populated from `EmployeeSession.Current.EmployeeId` in `FrmLogFeedback` → `LogFeedbackViewModel`. Persisted as the `LoggedBy` int and the `LoggedByEmployee` nav.

That's your "who made the feedback."

### 2. Who requested the feedback? → ⚠️ That's the customer, and it's `CustomerId`

Careful here, because "requested the feedback" is ambiguous in a way that matters.

- If "requested" means **"the customer this ticket is about"** — the person who gave the feedback — then yes, `CustomerId` + `Customer` nav. Fully covered.
- If "requested" means **"who initiated the logging"** — the staff member who opened the modal and filled it in — then that's `LoggedBy` again, same as #1.
- If "requested" means **"did the customer ask for service recovery?"** — there's no concept of that. The customer doesn't request anything in this domain; staff log feedback *about* their experience. There's no "customer-initiated request" object anywhere.

Given your earlier reframing ("who requested would be who was the customer"), I read #2 as the first meaning: **the customer the ticket concerns.** That's `CustomerId`, ✅ covered.

**Worth noting though:** in the Feedback flow, the customer isn't the one who "requested" anything in the domain's sense. Staff log the ticket. The customer is the *subject*. If a defense examiner asks "who requested this feedback ticket," the honest answer is "staff logged it about the customer; the customer didn't request anything." Whether that's an issue depends on how strictly the word "request" is being applied.

### 3. Who validated? → ✅ `DecidedBy` + `DecidedAt` (now, since your edit)

The employee who resolved or dismissed the ticket. Set in `MarkAsResolved(resolvedByEmployeeId, ...)` and `Dismiss(dismissedByEmployeeId, ...)` — both of which write `DecidedBy` and `DecidedAt`. Persisted as `DecidedBy` int, `DecidedAt` timestamp, plus the `DecidedByEmployee` nav.

That's your "who validated."

## The one honest gap worth stating

The word **"requested"** in your three questions doesn't map cleanly onto Feedback the way it maps onto `PointAdjustmentRequest`.

In `PointAdjustmentRequest`:

- `RequestedBy` = the employee who asked for the change
- `CustomerId` = the customer affected by the change
- `ApprovedBy` = the employee who approved/rejected

Clean three-way split: requester / subject / validator.

In `Feedback`:

- `LoggedBy` = the employee who logged the ticket
- `CustomerId` = the customer the ticket is about
- `DecidedBy` = the employee who decided

It's the same three-role structure, but the label "requester" doesn't fit Feedback because staff aren't requesting anything — they're recording. The right vocabulary for Feedback is **logger / subject / decider**, and it's fully covered.

**For a defense, the cleanest way to state it:** "Every feedback ticket records who logged it, when, which customer it concerns, and once a decision is made, who decided and when — with the decision's notes. That covers attribution end-to-end."

If someone pushes on the word "requested," you point out that Feedback isn't a request-based workflow (unlike point adjustments) — it's a record-with-decision workflow, and the three roles map to `LoggedBy` / `CustomerId` / `DecidedBy`.


**What you should see:** three new columns on `Feedbacks` — `DecidedBy` (nullable int), `DecidedAt` (nullable datetime2), `DecisionNotes` (nullable nvarchar(500)) — plus a foreign key from `Feedbacks.DecidedBy` → `Employees.EmployeeId`. No tables added, no columns dropped, no existing columns altered.

**What to check before moving on:** open the generated `Up()` method in the new migration file and confirm:

1. `AddColumn<int>(name: "DecidedBy", table: "Feedbacks", nullable: true)` — **`nullable: true` is critical**
2. `AddColumn<DateTime>(name: "DecidedAt", table: "Feedbacks", nullable: true)`
3. `AddColumn<string>(name: "DecisionNotes", table: "Feedbacks", nullable: true, maxLength: 500)`
4. `CreateIndex` and `AddForeignKey` for the `DecidedBy` → `Employees` relationship, with `onDelete: ReferentialAction.Restrict`
5. **Nothing else.** If the generated diff includes changes you didn't expect — column type changes, index drops, anything on other tables — **stop and paste it here.** That would mean the model drifted from the last migration in ways that weren't part of this session's work, and applying it blind could touch the live DB in ways you didn't intend.

But if the model had drifted before this session — say, from work in a previous session that never got migrated — then `migrations add` will scoop those changes into *this* migration too, and `database update` would apply all of it. So verify the diff is only the three columns + FK before proceeding.

If it fails, the most likely causes are (a) the connection string can't reach the hosted DB, (b) a permissions issue on the DB user, or (c) the DB already has the columns from an out-of-band change — in which case you'd see a "column already exists" error and we'd need to look at the migration's `Up()` again.

## What I understand from the updated plan

**The big shift since I last saw this file:** the DB-connection workstream is no longer "WinForms talks directly to EF Core." It's now **WinForms → HTTP (JWT) → `CRM_Morcaffein.api` → EF Core → SQL Server.** That's a much bigger architectural decision than the earlier conversation implied, and it changes a lot of what I'd assumed. Specifically:

- The API project becomes a real, live component — not just the place migrations are generated from.
- There's now an **auth layer** (JWT + POST /auth/login), which pulls FrmLogin back into scope as a real deliverable rather than a permanently-deferred stub.
- The WinForms app gets **API client services** (`Api*Service`) that implement the exact same `I*Service` interfaces the mocks implement today. Which means — as the plan notes — the swap is contained to `ServiceRegistry.cs` plus the new `Api*Service` classes, and no ViewModel or View changes.
- **Multitenancy is deferred** — hardcode tenant A for now. Good call; building master-DB tenant lookup with one real tenant is over-engineering.

**The one structural blocker:** the `I*Service` interfaces currently live in the WinForms project, but the API project can't reference WinForms (WinForms already references the API → circular). So the interfaces have to move into `CRM_Morcaffein.infrastructure` (which both sides already reference), keeping their `namespace CRM_Morcaffein.Services;` declaration so nothing else breaks. That's step 0, before anything else. I agree with that move — it's the cleanest way to share contracts without a fifth project, and the namespace trick means zero downstream changes.

**The sequencing:** 0 (scaffolding + interface move + JWT + ApiClient + FrmLogin) → 1 (Customers) → 2 (Feedback) → 3 (Campaigns/PointAdjustments, where server-side role enforcement lands) → 4 (Products/Orders, most complex, last) → 5 (cleanup: delete mocks + PrivateSetterAccessor).

**Why gradual:** ServiceRegistry's properties are independent, each View only depends on its own interface, so you can swap one line at a time and both halves keep working. I agree with this — big-bang swaps are how you spend a week debugging six moving parts with no working baseline.

## Things I want to discuss before we go further

**1. Does the API layer change the "save timing" question?**

With direct EF, I'd argued for deferred save (one `SaveChanges` per logical operation). With HTTP in the middle, that question mostly dissolves — each HTTP request is a round-trip, and the API endpoint decides when to save. So the real question becomes: **does the POS build up a cart server-side (many small mutations, each a POST), or does the WinForms app hold the cart client-side and POST the whole order once at "Log Sale"?**

That's a meaningful design choice, and it's not in the plan. Consequences:

- **Client-side cart:** fast, no network per item, no half-saved orders. But the "order" isn't persisted until checkout, so there's no server-side record of in-progress sales, and if the terminal crashes mid-sale, the cart is gone. For a POS this is probably fine.
- **Server-side cart:** every AddItem is a POST, order exists server-side as Pending, could be resumed from another terminal, but every tap is a network round-trip and a half-built order sits in the DB.

**My instinct: client-side cart, POST once on Log Sale.** Matches how the current `TransactionViewModel` works, and a POS cart doesn't need server persistence. But this is a decision, not a default — worth adding to the plan.

**2. Where does "Products" fit in the sequencing?**

The plan sequences Products/Orders together as step 4 (most complex, last). But **Products is mostly reads** — `GetCategories`, `GetProducts`, `GetByCategory`, `GetById`, `GetModifiers`. Splitting them: **Products as its own simple step (after Feedback, before Campaigns), and Orders as the final complex step on its own.** That way the "simple service first" pattern gets one more rep before the hard one. Worth considering.

**3. When does the menu revision land relative to this?**

The menu spec we wrote is a **data** change — new `Product`/`ProductSize`/`ProductModifier` seed data. But with the API in the middle, the seed data lives server-side in the real DB. So the question is:

This matters because the plan file lists the menu revision as "deferred, owner's next plan" but doesn't say *when* — and the answer depends on whether you want to see the new menu in the app before the DB swap, or wait.
