**1. Size buttons now recompute on resize.** `OnResize` calls `RecomputeSizeButtonRects()`. When the TableLayoutPanel gives the card its actual width, the rects get recalculated and the buttons fill the full width.

**2. Images now "cover" the top area.** Instead of fitting with letterboxing, the image scales up so it fills the entire image area, centered, with the overflow clipped. **This is what makes it look modern** — no empty bands on the sides or top.

**3. Card is taller.** `Size = new Size(150, 200)` — the image gets significantly more room. Combined with the TableLayoutPanel's `Dock = Fill`, the card uses whatever width the cell gives it. **You'll need to update the row height in `RefreshProductsPanel`** — it's currently `172f`, change to something like `216f` (200 + margins).

**4. Larger placeholder glyph.** `IconFont(28f)` — the ☕ is bigger when there's no image.

## Change in `RefreshProductsPanel`

Find:

```csharp
_productsGrid.RowStyles.Add(new RowStyle(SizeType.Absolute, 172f));   // card height + margin
```

## About the progressive rendering

I've been assuming the progressive fill is caused by the layout mechanism. But we just switched to `TableLayoutPanel` — which lays out in a single pass — and it's *still* progressive.

**At this point, the progressive fill is not a layout problem. It's how Windows draws.** When you `ResumeRedraw` and the panel becomes visible, Windows paints the client area in horizontal bands as the message loop processes WM_PAINT. Even a single `Invalidate` paint can appear progressive if there's enough content to paint.

**Two things can still help:**

**A. Draw a snapshot instead of live cards.** Render the entire grid to a `Bitmap` once, then paint the bitmap in one `OnPaint`. The user sees the whole bitmap at once. But then you lose interactivity (hit-testing on the bitmap). Not viable for cards with buttons.

**B. Accept that it's a Windows rendering characteristic, and just make sure it's fast enough to not be noticed.** Which we've been doing. With the new optimizations (no per-paint allocations, Bilinear, TextRenderer), 34 cards should paint in ~100-200ms — noticeable but not the "lots of cards filling in over a second" that you described earlier.

Fair. Let me explain how tab order actually works in your codebase, then propose how to fix all of them consistently.

## Why it's out of order

WinForms tab order is set by each control's `TabIndex` property. When you don't set it explicitly, WinForms uses the order the controls were **added to their parent** — starting at 0 and incrementing.

**Your controls are added in whatever order the code builds them.** Looking at the code you've pasted, that's why it's broken:

- In `BuildCustomerColumn`, controls are added **bottom-up** on purpose (so the docking stack looks right): `_customerProfilePanel`, `_customerSearchErrorLabel`, `searchRow`, `promoRow`. But the **visual** order top-to-bottom is: `searchRow`, `_customerSearchErrorLabel`, `_customerProfilePanel`, `promoRow`. So the tab order is reversed.
- In `FrmLogin`, the right-pane controls are added: `_loginBtn`, `_errorLabel`, `_passwordTxtBx`, `passwordLabel`, `_usernameTxtBx`, `usernameLabel`, `hintLabel`, `headingLabel`. Visual order is the opposite.

**Reverse-add-order is the pattern used throughout your app for docking to work correctly.** It's correct for layout, but it's the exact opposite of what tab order wants.

## The fix pattern

After building a container's children, **explicitly set `TabIndex` on each control in the desired tab order.** WinForms respects explicit `TabIndex` values regardless of add-order.

For example, in `BuildCustomerColumn`, after all the `column.Controls.Add(...)` calls:

```csharp
column.Controls.Add(_customerProfilePanel);
column.Controls.Add(_customerSearchErrorLabel);
column.Controls.Add(searchRow);
column.Controls.Add(promoRow);

// Explicit tab order — visual top-to-bottom, not add-order.
_customerSearchTxtBx.TabIndex = 0;
_customerSearchErrorLabel.TabIndex = 1;   // doesn't receive focus (Label) but keeps things consistent
_customerProfilePanel.TabIndex = 2;       // ditto
_promoMenuBtn.TabIndex = 3;
```

**Do this for every container that has interactive children.**

## What counts as "interactive"

Only controls that can receive focus matter for tab order: `TextBox`, `Button`, `CheckBox`, `RadioButton`, `ComboBox`, `NumericUpDown`, `DataGridView`, custom UserControls with `TabStop = true`.

**Labels are `TabStop = false` by default** — they never receive focus. Setting their TabIndex is technically harmless but doesn't affect tab behavior. So we only need to tab-order the focusable controls.

That means the actual work per screen is smaller than it looks — usually 3-8 controls.

## The plan

For each screen, I'll:

1. Identify the focusable controls in their container.
2. Set their `TabIndex` explicitly, in the visual top-to-bottom / left-to-right order.
3. Ensure `TabStop = true` on the ones that should be focusable (some are set to `false` by default; DataGridView is `true` by default, but its cells need `TabStop` too).

## What I need from you

**Confirm you want me to do all of the following, one at a time, in order:**

1. **FrmLogin** — username, password, Log In button. **(3 controls.)**
2. **FrmCustomerOnboarding** — first name, last name, phone, email, birthday checkbox, birthday picker, Cancel, Next, Back, Confirm.
3. **FrmLogFeedback** — customer search, customer list, star rating, category combo, notes, Cancel, Next, Back, Submit.
4. **FrmItemCustomizer** — size radios, modifier checkboxes, quantity stepper buttons, Add to Cart, Cancel.
5. **TransactionView** — customer search box, Go button, product search, category combo, promo button, drink cards (each is a single custom control — needs its own TabStop/TabIndex treatment), cart line steppers, Log Sale button.
6. **CustomerManagementView** — search box, New Customer button, grid, drawer's request form controls, approve/reject buttons.
7. **FeedbackManagementView** — search box, Log Feedback button, grid, Cancel Ticket button.

**Say "go" and start with FrmLogin, or pick a different order.**

Some of these are quick (FrmLogin is 30 seconds). Some are more involved (TransactionView, since custom controls like ProductCardControl need to expose their own tab stop).

**One thing to flag:** for `ProductCardControl` and `CartLineControl` (custom UserControls), making them focusable requires more than just setting `TabIndex`. They need `TabStop = true`, and they need to handle keyboard input (Enter to open the customizer, arrow keys for navigation). That's a bigger design decision — I'd suggest we leave custom controls out of the tab order for now (POS is mouse-driven anyway) and just fix the standard inputs.

**If you agree, our scope is: TextBox, Button, CheckBox, RadioButton, ComboBox, NumericUpDown controls across all 7 screens.**

# Tab order — FrmCustomerOnboarding

Open `CRM_Morcaffein.winforms/Views/FrmCustomerOnboarding.cs` (the code-behind, not the Designer).

## The controls and their desired tab order

Looking at your Designer file earlier, the focusable controls are:

1. `firstNameTxtBx` — first name
2. `lastNameTxtBx` — last name
3. `phoneTxtBx` — phone
4. `emailTxtBx` — email
5. `hasBirthdayChk` — "Birthday on file" checkbox
6. `birthdayPicker` — date picker (disabled until the checkbox is ticked)
7. `cancelBtn` — Cancel (step 1 only)
8. `nextBtn` — Next (step 1 only)
9. `backBtn` — Back (step 2 only)
10. `confirmBtn` — Confirm (step 2 only)

## Where to add the TabIndex lines

The form is built in the Designer, so all 10 controls exist after `InitializeComponent()` runs. You can set their `TabIndex` in the constructor, right after `InitializeComponent();`.

Find this in the constructor:

```csharp
public FrmCustomerOnboarding(CustomerController controller)
{
    _controller = controller;
    InitializeComponent();

    hasBirthdayChk.CheckedChanged += (s, e) => { ... };
    // ... other event wiring ...
}
```

**Add right after `InitializeComponent();`:**

```csharp
// Explicit tab order — visual top-to-bottom, left-to-right.
// Step 1 order: first name -> last name -> phone -> email -> birthday -> Cancel -> Next.
// Step 2 order: Back -> Confirm (Next and Cancel are hidden on step 2).
firstNameTxtBx.TabIndex = 0;
lastNameTxtBx.TabIndex = 1;
phoneTxtBx.TabIndex = 2;
emailTxtBx.TabIndex = 3;
hasBirthdayChk.TabIndex = 4;
birthdayPicker.TabIndex = 5;
cancelBtn.TabIndex = 6;
nextBtn.TabIndex = 7;
backBtn.TabIndex = 8;
confirmBtn.TabIndex = 9;
```

## What this does

- **Step 1 tab flow:** first name → last name → phone → email → birthday checkbox → birthday picker → Cancel → Next. Then it wraps back to first name.
- **Step 2 tab flow:** when Next is clicked, first four fields and Cancel/Next are hidden. The visible controls are Back and Confirm. WinForms skips hidden controls when tabbing. So on step 2, tab goes: Back → Confirm → (loops to) Back.

**Note about the birthday picker:** when the checkbox isn't ticked, `birthdayPicker.Enabled = false`. Disabled controls are skipped by the tab traversal too. So the flow is: first name → last name → phone → email → birthday checkbox → (skips picker if disabled) → Cancel → Next.

## Apply and verify

1. Add the 10 lines right after `InitializeComponent();` in the constructor.
2. Rebuild, run.
3. Open "+ New Customer".
4. Press Tab through the fields. Should follow the order above.

**One thing that might feel off:** if you'd rather have Next BEFORE Cancel (which is more common in wizards), swap their TabIndex values:

```csharp
nextBtn.TabIndex = 6;
cancelBtn.TabIndex = 7;
```

My default put Cancel first because it's on the left side of the button row (visually left-to-right). But if you tab through and it feels wrong, swap them.

# Tab order — FrmItemCustomizer

This one's different from the previous two — it's a **code-built form** (no Designer file). All controls are created in the constructor. That means we can set `TabIndex` right after each control is created, or in one block near the end of the constructor.

Open `CRM_Morcaffein.winforms/Views/FrmItemCustomizer.cs`.

## The focusable controls

Looking at the file you sent earlier:

- **Size radios** — created in `BuildSizeOptions()`, one per product size (up to 3 typically). Currently stored in `_sizePanel`.
- **Modifier checkboxes** — created in `BuildModifierOptions()`, one per modifier. Currently stored in `_modifiersPanel`.
- **Qty stepper** — `minusBtn` and `plusBtn` in `BuildQuantityStepper()`.
- **`_confirmBtn`** — the primary action button.
- **`cancelBtn`** — the cancel button.

## Where to add the TabIndex lines

The layout is: name → size radios → modifier checkboxes → qty stepper → price → buttons. Visual top-to-bottom.

**Find where the controls are added to the form** — near the end of the constructor, before `RefreshPriceLabel()`:

```csharp
Controls.Add(_priceLabel);
Controls.Add(qtyRow);
Controls.Add(qtyHeader);
Controls.Add(_modifiersPanel);
Controls.Add(modifierHeader);
Controls.Add(_sizePanel);
Controls.Add(sizeHeader);
Controls.Add(productNameLabel);
Controls.Add(cancelBtn);
Controls.Add(_confirmBtn);

RefreshPriceLabel();
```

**Add this block right after the `Controls.Add(...)` calls, before `RefreshPriceLabel();`:**

```csharp
// Explicit tab order — visual top-to-bottom.
// WinForms doesn't naturally sort tab-order by position; since we add controls in
// reverse for correct docking, we set TabIndex explicitly here.
//
// Order: size radios (top-down), then modifier checkboxes (top-down),
// then the qty stepper (-/+), then Cancel, then Add to Cart.

// Size radios
var sizeRadios = _sizePanel.Controls.OfType<RadioButton>().ToList();
// Note: BuildSizeOptions reversed the child order so they display top-to-bottom.
// _sizePanel.Controls order after the reverse is TOP-first, so iterate normally.
for (int i = 0; i < sizeRadios.Count; i++)
{
    // Since _sizePanel.Controls order matches visual order (after the reverse), this
    // gives radios tab-order equal to visual order.
    sizeRadios[i].TabIndex = i;
}

// Modifier checkboxes — same logic, they were also reversed in BuildModifierOptions
var modChecks = _modifiersPanel.Controls.OfType<CheckBox>().ToList();
for (int i = 0; i < modChecks.Count; i++)
{
    modChecks[i].TabIndex = 100 + i;
}

// Stepper buttons and the rest of the form — use a high base so they come after
// all radios and checkboxes regardless of how many sizes/modifiers there are.
var stepperButtons = qtyRow.Controls.OfType<Button>().ToList();
// The stepper buttons are added in order: minusBtn, _qtyValueLabel, plusBtn.
// We want minus -> plus (skip the label; it's not focusable).
for (int i = 0; i < stepperButtons.Count; i++)
{
    stepperButtons[i].TabIndex = 1000 + i;
}

cancelBtn.TabIndex = 2000;
_confirmBtn.TabIndex = 2001;
```

**Wait — there's a problem with this approach.** The `TabIndex` values for controls in different parent containers don't compete with each other. WinForms uses a hierarchical tab system: within each container, children are ordered by their own TabIndex. Then the **container's** TabIndex determines where its whole subtree fits in the outer tab order.

So `_sizePanel` and `_modifiersPanel` need their own TabIndex on the form itself, and the controls inside them need relative TabIndex within their panels. Trying to give a checkbox inside `_modifiersPanel` a TabIndex of `100 + i` doesn't do anything to the outer tab order — it just orders the checkboxes within `_modifiersPanel`, which they already are.

## The correct fix

**Two steps:**

**Step A — order the containers on the form.** The form's controls (containers and standalone controls) need their TabIndex set in visual order.

**Step B — order the focusable controls within each container.** Radios in `_sizePanel`, checkboxes in `_modifiersPanel`, buttons in `qtyRow`.

**Replace my block above with this:**

```csharp
// Tab order — hierarchical. Set the CONTAINER order on the form first, then the
// focusable children within each container.

// --- Containers and standalone focusable controls on the form ---
// Visual order: size panel -> modifiers panel -> qty row -> cancel -> confirm
_sizePanel.TabIndex = 0;
_modifiersPanel.TabIndex = 1;
qtyRow.TabIndex = 2;
cancelBtn.TabIndex = 3;
_confirmBtn.TabIndex = 4;

// Non-focusable labels don't need a TabIndex but we set them anyway to keep the
// form's internal ordering tidy. Labels are TabStop=false so they're skipped.
productNameLabel.TabIndex = 5;
sizeHeader.TabIndex = 6;
modifierHeader.TabIndex = 7;
qtyHeader.TabIndex = 8;
_priceLabel.TabIndex = 9;

// --- Focusable controls within each container ---
// Size radios: top-to-bottom matches the order they appear in _sizePanel.Controls
// after BuildSizeOptions reversed them.
var sizeRadios = _sizePanel.Controls.OfType<RadioButton>().ToList();
for (int i = 0; i < sizeRadios.Count; i++)
    sizeRadios[i].TabIndex = i;

// Modifier checkboxes: same logic.
var modChecks = _modifiersPanel.Controls.OfType<CheckBox>().ToList();
for (int i = 0; i < modChecks.Count; i++)
    modChecks[i].TabIndex = i;

// Qty stepper buttons: minus, then plus (skip the qty label — not focusable).
// Qty row adds in order: minusBtn, _qtyValueLabel, plusBtn.
var stepperButtons = qtyRow.Controls.OfType<Button>().ToList();
for (int i = 0; i < stepperButtons.Count; i++)
    stepperButtons[i].TabIndex = i;
```

## What the tab flow becomes

1. First size radio (S / Regular) — selected
2. Down arrow or Tab → next size radio
3. After all sizes → first modifier checkbox
4. Tab through all modifier checkboxes
5. After last modifier → minus button
6. Tab → plus button
7. Tab → Cancel button
8. Tab → Add to Cart button
9. Tab wraps back to first size radio

**What's skipped:** labels, the price label, headers. They're all `TabStop = false`.

## Apply and verify

1. Add the block above right after the existing `Controls.Add(...)` calls, before `RefreshPriceLabel();`.
2. Rebuild, run.
3. Open Transactions, search a customer, click a drink card body to open the customizer.
4. Tab through the modal. Should follow the flow above.

**One note about sizes and radios:** radio buttons inside a panel are tabbed as a **group** by default. Pressing Tab moves to the *next group* (i.e. to the first modifier checkbox), and arrow keys move between radios *within* the group. So the actual behavior might be:

- Tab lands on the currently-selected size radio.
- Arrow keys change the selected size (up/down).
- Tab moves to the first modifier checkbox.

That's actually the correct WinForms behavior — better than tabbing through every radio. **If that's what happens, it's fine and expected.**

## The approval-split correction

**Manager customer editing — yes to both means:**

The Manager **can** edit the customer record — the change applies immediately to the record. **AND** the edit is also submitted as a request that Admin can review (and approve or reject). So the flow is:

1. Manager edits a customer's record (e.g. changes phone number).
2. The change is **live immediately** — the record shows the new value.
3. **Simultaneously**, a request is queued for Admin review.
4. Admin can approve (no-op — the change is already applied) or **reject** — in which case the record **reverts** to the previous value.

**Confirm this is the model**, because it has significant implications:

- The system must store the **previous value** alongside the new one, to support reverting on rejection.
- "Approve" is a no-op (nothing changes — the edit is already live).
- "Reject" triggers a revert.
- This differs from the point-adjustment model, where the change only applies *after* approval.

**Same for campaign creation?** Manager creates a campaign → goes live immediately → sits in Admin's queue → Admin can reject → campaign is deactivated/reverted. Confirm.

**If those are right, the rule is:**

- **Point adjustments (both staff→manager and manager→admin):** change applies *after* approval. Blocked until approved.
- **Customer edits and campaign creation (manager→admin):** change applies *immediately*; Admin can reject to reverse.

That's a meaningfully different approval model per action type, and I want to make sure it's correct before writing it into the plan. Confirm or correct.

- **Near the next tier** = sends when a customer is, say, 20 points away from Silver or Gold. Only fires when a tier upgrade is imminent. More targeted.

```text
1. WHAT THIS PROJECT IS
====================================================================
A Coffee Shop Loyalty & Retention CRM ("Morcaffein") — a WinForms desktop app
(.NET, net10.0-windows) for the STAFF side of the business, backed by a real EF
Core + SQL Server database accessed through a web API (CRM_Morcaffein.api).

The system has four roles: Barista (staff), Manager, Admin, and SuperAdmin.
The Staff/Manager/Admin UIs live in the WinForms app; SuperAdmin is the
developer and operates at the infrastructure level (no login in the app).

Current state: the Staff UI (all three pillars) is fully API-backed and
working. Login is functional. The Manager and Admin UIs are not yet built.

====================================================================
2. ARCHITECTURE / STACK DECISIONS
====================================================================
- WinForms, not WPF.
- MVC, not MVVM. Controllers are plain classes:
    * WinForms side: Controllers/*.cs — UI controllers that read inputs, call
      the API, update controls. No bindable properties, no commands.
    * API side: CRM_Morcaffein.api/Controllers/*.cs — [ApiController] classes
      that contain ALL business rules and persistence.
  Common/ObservableObject.cs and Common/RelayCommand.cs are deleted.

- Domain entities in CRM_Morcaffein.domain/entities. Mostly public-set
  properties. Business rules moved to the API controllers.

- EF Core 10 with TWO contexts:
    * MasterCrmDbContext (multitenant: Companies, CompanyDatabases, Devices)
    * TenantCrmDbContext (per-tenant: Customers, Orders, Products, etc.)

- Multitenant setup:
    * Master DB maps CompanyId -> tenant DB info.
    * Currently three tenants exist (A/B/C), but the app hardcodes tenant A
      (companyId = 1) via ApiConfig.CompanyId on the client.
    * Cross-tenant middleware (rejecting requests where the JWT's companyId

- Client -> API -> DB flow:

             ->  EF Core  ->  SQL Server (LocalDB for local dev)

- Local DB cutover: the runtime now points at (localdb)\MSSQLLocalDB (both
  master and tenant). Cloud connection strings (MonsterASP) preserved in
  appsettings.json for later sync / demo work.

- Design-time factory for migrations: TenantCrmDbContextFactory.cs and
  MasterCrmDbContextFactory.cs in infrastructure/data/, with hardcoded
  LocalDB connection strings. Only used by `dotnet ef`.

- Runtime tenant factory: TenantDbContextFactory.cs in infrastructure/services/
  branches on whether the resolved ServerName contains "(localdb)": if so,
  uses Trusted_Connection=True (Windows auth); otherwise uses the credential
  lookup from appsettings.json.

====================================================================

ROLE ORDER
    Barista  <  Manager  <  Admin  <  SuperAdmin

WHAT EACH ROLE IS
    - Barista: the primary counter staff. Ring sales, look up customers,
      log feedback, request point adjustments.
    - Manager: runs the shift. Approves staff point adjustments, resolves
      feedback, manages campaigns, edits customer records, sees the
      dashboard, exports reports to PDF.
    - Admin: supervises the tenant. Approves Manager actions (point
      adjustments, customer edits, campaign creation). Manages users

    - SuperAdmin: the developer. No login in the app. Operates at the
      infrastructure level (creating tenants via the API, managing the
      master DB). The SuperAdmin x Admin UI surface is deferred.

====================================================================
4. APPROVAL MODEL
====================================================================
Two approval chains, with different mechanics per action type:

CHAIN A — STAFF -> MANAGER (blocked until approved)
    * Point adjustments requested by staff.
      Manager approves or rejects. Approval applies the change; rejection
      closes the request with no change.

CHAIN B — MANAGER -> ADMIN (split by action type)

    B1. POINT ADJUSTMENTS — BLOCKED UNTIL APPROVED
        Manager requests a point adjustment. Admin approves (change applies)
        or rejects (no change). Same mechanic as Chain A.

    B2. CUSTOMER EDITS — APPLIES IMMEDIATELY, ADMIN CAN REVERSE
        Manager edits a customer record. The change is written to the DB
        immediately (visible to everyone). Simultaneously a review request is
        queued for Admin. Admin can approve (no-op — already applied) or
        reject, in which case the record REVERTS to its previous value.

    B3. CAMPAIGN CREATION — BLOCKED UNTIL APPROVED
        Manager creates a campaign. It does NOT go live until Admin approves.
        Admin rejection cancels the campaign.

    B4. SUBSCRIPTIONS — deferred (out of scope for now).

RULES
    * An employee can NEVER approve their own request.
    * Every approval/rejection records DecidedBy, DecidedAt, DecisionNotes
      (on the respective entity).
    * Rejections require a reason. Approvals may have optional notes.

ADMIN (not yet built)

SUPERADMIN (deferred)

NEW sidebar tab, visible to Manager and Admin only. Barista does not see it.

CONTENT (initial)

Provider: deferred. The provider will be decided later; for now, only the

TRIGGERS
    A) New promotion (campaign activated)

WORK ORDER (relative to other workstreams)
```

## File 2 — `CRM_Morcaffein.winforms/Views/Controls/PlaceholderView.cs` (new)

A single reusable placeholder view. Takes a title and description in the constructor.

```csharp
using CRM_Morcaffein.Theme;

namespace CRM_Morcaffein.winforms.Views.Controls
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Reusable placeholder for tabs that don't have their real UI yet.
    /// Shows a centered title + short description.
    /// </summary>
    public class PlaceholderView : UserControl
    {
        public PlaceholderView(string title, string description)
        {
            Dock = DockStyle.Fill;
            BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfaceSecondary;

            var card = new Panel
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Fill,
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfacePrimary,
                Padding = new Padding(24),
                Margin = new Padding(24),
            };

            var titleLabel = new Label
            {
                Text = title,
                Dock = DockStyle.Top,
                Height = 40,
                TextAlign = ContentAlignment.MiddleCenter,
                Font = BrandPalette.BrandFontBold(20f),
                ForeColor = BrandPalette.NeutralText,
            };

            var descriptionLabel = new Label
            {
                Text = description,
                Dock = DockStyle.Top,
                Height = 60,
                TextAlign = ContentAlignment.MiddleCenter,
                Font = BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(10.5f),
                ForeColor = BrandPalette.NeutralTextMuted,
            };

            var spacer = new Panel { Dock = DockStyle.Top, Height = 80 };

            card.Controls.Add(descriptionLabel);
            card.Controls.Add(titleLabel);
            card.Controls.Add(spacer);

            var outer = new Panel
            {
                Dock = DockStyle.Fill,
                BackColor = BrandPalette.SurfaceSecondary,
                Padding = new Padding(24),
            };
            outer.Controls.Add(card);

            Controls.Add(outer);
        }
    }
}
```

**What it does:** centered title + description on a white card. Used for all the placeholder tabs.

## File 3 — `FrmMain.cs` rewrite

The sidebar nav needs to be built dynamically. Here's the full replacement. I'm working from the structure you sent earlier.

```csharp
using CRM_Morcaffein.Session;
using CRM_Morcaffein.Theme;
using CRM_Morcaffein.winforms.Views.Controls;

namespace CRM_Morcaffein.winforms.Views
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Staff console shell: a right-docked nav strip and a content area that swaps in
    /// whichever tab is active. The nav items shown depend on the logged-in employee's
    /// role:
    ///   Barista → Transactions, Customers, Feedback
    ///   Manager → Dashboard, Campaign, Customers, Feedback
    ///   Admin   → Dashboard, Approvals, Manage Users
    ///
    /// Customers and Feedback reuse the same views across roles that have them.
    /// Placeholder tabs (Dashboard, Campaign, Approvals, Manage Users) use PlaceholderView.
    /// </summary>
    public partial class FrmMain : Form
    {
        public FrmMain()
        {
            InitializeComponent();

            // Login already seeded EmployeeSession before this form was launched.
            var employee = EmployeeSession.Current!.Employee;
            staffNameLabel.Text = employee.FullName;
            staffRoleLabel.Text = employee.Role;
            avatarPanel.Paint += AvatarPanel_Paint;
            brandMarkPanel.Paint += BrandMarkPanel_Paint;

            BuildNavButtons(employee.Role);

            logoutBtn.Click += LogoutBtn_Click;
        }

        private void FrmMain_Load(object sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            // Activate the first nav button that was built for this role.
            if (sidebarPanel.Controls.OfType<Button>().Any())
            {
                var firstNav = sidebarPanel.Controls.OfType<Button>().First();
                firstNav.PerformClick();
            }
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Builds the sidebar nav buttons based on the employee's role.
        /// </summary>
        private void BuildNavButtons(string role)
        {
            var isManager = role.Equals("Manager", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                            role.Equals("Admin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                            role.Equals("SuperAdmin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
            var isAdmin = role.Equals("Admin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                          role.Equals("SuperAdmin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

            var navItems = new List<(string Text, Action onClick)>();

            if (isAdmin)
            {
                navItems.Add(("Dashboard", () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Dashboard",
                    "Business intelligence and reports. Coming soon."))));
                navItems.Add(("Approvals", () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Approvals",
                    "Review and approve Manager actions — point adjustments, customer edits, campaign creations. Coming soon."))));
                navItems.Add(("Manage Users", () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Manage Users",
                    "Create, edit, and deactivate employee accounts. Coming soon."))));
            }
            else if (isManager)
            {
                navItems.Add(("Dashboard", () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Dashboard",
                    "Business intelligence and reports. Coming soon."))));
                navItems.Add(("Campaign", () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Campaign",
                    "Create and manage campaigns, activate promos, send SMS notifications. Coming soon."))));
                navItems.Add(("Customers", () => ShowView(new CustomerManagementView())));
                navItems.Add(("Feedback", () => ShowView(new FeedbackManagementView())));
            }
            else
            {
                // Barista (default)
                navItems.Add(("Transactions", () => ShowView(new TransactionView())));
                navItems.Add(("Customers", () => ShowView(new CustomerManagementView())));
                navItems.Add(("Feedback", () => ShowView(new FeedbackManagementView())));
            }

            // Build the buttons. Layout from top of sidebar, stacked vertically.
            // The Designer originally placed three hardcoded buttons at fixed positions.
            // Here we replace that with a runtime loop.
            int y = 20;
            const int buttonWidth = 184;
            const int buttonHeight = 46;
            const int gap = 12;

            foreach (var (text, onClick) in navItems)
            {
                var btn = new Button
                {
                    Text = text,
                    Size = new Size(buttonWidth, buttonHeight),
                    Location = new Point(18, y),
                };
                StyleNavButton(btn, active: false);

                var capturedOnClick = onClick;
                btn.Click += (s, e) =>
                {
                    SetActiveNav(btn);
                    topBarTabLabel.Text = "/ " + text;
                    capturedOnClick();
                };

                sidebarPanel.Controls.Add(btn);
                y += buttonHeight + gap;
            }
        }

        private void ShowView(UserControl view)
        {
            contentPanel.Controls.Clear();
            view.Dock = DockStyle.Fill;
            contentPanel.Controls.Add(view);
        }

        private void SetActiveNav(Button active)
        {
            foreach (var button in sidebarPanel.Controls.OfType<Button>())
            {
                // Skip the logout button if it's in the sidebar (it usually lives in the footer, not the sidebar).
                if (button == logoutBtn) continue;

                button.BackColor = button == active ? BrandPalette.NavActiveBackground : BrandPalette.NavBackground;
                button.ForeColor = button == active ? BrandPalette.NavActiveText : BrandPalette.NavText;
                button.Font = button == active ? BrandPalette.BrandFontBold(10f) : BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(10f);
            }
        }

        private void LogoutBtn_Click(object? sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            var confirm = MessageBox.Show(this,
                $"Log out of {EmployeeSession.Current?.DisplayName}'s session?",
                "Log Out", MessageBoxButtons.YesNo, MessageBoxIcon.Question);

            if (confirm != DialogResult.Yes)
                return;

            EmployeeSession.End();

            // Close this shell; Program.cs's Main will loop back to FrmLogin (once we update Program.cs).
            // For now, closing is the behavior — see the Program.cs note below.
            Close();
        }

        private void BrandMarkPanel_Paint(object? sender, PaintEventArgs e)
        {
            var g = e.Graphics;
            g.SmoothingMode = System.Drawing.Drawing2D.SmoothingMode.AntiAlias;

            using var brush = new SolidBrush(BrandPalette.Brand);
            g.FillEllipse(brush, 0, 0, brandMarkPanel.Width - 1, brandMarkPanel.Height - 1);

            using var font = BrandPalette.BrandFontBold(11f);
            var textSize = g.MeasureString("M", font);
            g.DrawString("M", font, Brushes.White,
                (brandMarkPanel.Width - textSize.Width) / 2, (brandMarkPanel.Height - textSize.Height) / 2);
        }

        private void AvatarPanel_Paint(object? sender, PaintEventArgs e)
        {
            var g = e.Graphics;
            g.SmoothingMode = System.Drawing.Drawing2D.SmoothingMode.AntiAlias;

            using var brush = new SolidBrush(BrandPalette.Brand);
            g.FillEllipse(brush, 0, 0, avatarPanel.Width - 1, avatarPanel.Height - 1);

            var initials = GetInitials(EmployeeSession.Current?.DisplayName);
            using var font = BrandPalette.BrandFontBold(11f);
            var textSize = g.MeasureString(initials, font);
            g.DrawString(initials, font, Brushes.White,
                (avatarPanel.Width - textSize.Width) / 2, (avatarPanel.Height - textSize.Height) / 2);
        }

        private static string GetInitials(string? fullName)
        {
            if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(fullName))
                return "?";

            var parts = fullName.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);
            return parts.Length switch
            {
                0 => "?",
                1 => parts[0][..1].ToUpperInvariant(),
                _ => (parts[0][..1] + parts[^1][..1]).ToUpperInvariant(),
            };
        }

        private static void StyleNavButton(Button button, bool active)
        {
            button.FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat;
            button.FlatAppearance.BorderSize = 0;
            button.TextAlign = ContentAlignment.MiddleLeft;
            button.Padding = new Padding(16, 0, 0, 0);
            button.Font = active ? BrandPalette.BrandFontBold(10f) : BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(10f);
            button.Cursor = Cursors.Hand;
            button.BackColor = active ? BrandPalette.NavActiveBackground : BrandPalette.NavBackground;
            button.ForeColor = active ? BrandPalette.NavActiveText : BrandPalette.NavText;
            button.FlatAppearance.MouseOverBackColor = BrandPalette.NavHoverBackground;
        }
    }
}
```

   - **B.** Keep them but hide them: `navTransactionsBtn.Visible = false;` etc., then build the dynamic nav on top.

## File 4 — Do we need to update `Program.cs`?

Currently `Program.cs` is:

```csharp
using var login = new FrmLogin();
if (login.ShowDialog() != DialogResult.OK)
    return;

Application.Run(new FrmMain());
```

**The logout path closes `FrmMain` and the app exits.** After logging out, you'd want to return to the login screen, not exit. That's a nicer UX.

**Fix — wrap in a loop:**

```csharp
using CRM_Morcaffein.winforms.Services.Api;
using CRM_Morcaffein.winforms.Views;

namespace CRM_Morcaffein
{
    internal static class Program
    {
        [STAThread]
        static void Main()
        {
            ApplicationConfiguration.Initialize();

            // Prewarm the API (fire-and-forget, ignore failures).
            _ = Task.Run(async () =>
            {
                try
                {
                    using var http = new HttpClient
                    {
                        BaseAddress = new Uri(ApiConfig.BaseUrl),
                        Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10),
                    };
                    await http.GetAsync($"api/tenant/{ApiConfig.CompanyId}/customers?page=1&pageSize=1");
                }
                catch { }
            });

            // Loop: show login, then main, until the user closes the login window.
            while (true)
            {
                using var login = new FrmLogin();
                if (login.ShowDialog() != DialogResult.OK)
                    return;   // user closed login — exit the app

                Application.Run(new FrmMain());

                // If FrmMain closed, loop back to login. If the user closed FrmMain manually
                // (not via logout), we still loop back — which is the right behavior.
            }
        }
    }
}
```

**What changes:** the app loops. After logout, `FrmMain` closes, `Application.Run` returns, and the loop shows `FrmLogin` again. The user can log in as a different role without restarting the app. **This is important for testing RBAC** — you can flip between Barista and Manager by logging out and back in.

Fair — I hardcoded a hash that doesn't match. Two problems to fix.

## Immediate: unlock the accounts and reset them to plaintext

In SSMS against the **local tenant DB**:

```sql
UPDATE Credentials
SET PasswordHash = 'password123',
    FailedLoginAttempts = 0,
    IsLocked = 0
WHERE Username IN ('ana.barista', 'marco.manager');
```

**This puts the two new accounts back to plaintext `password123`.** Also check that Renz's account isn't locked from the failed attempts (you may have tried to log in as Renz and failed):

```sql
UPDATE Credentials
SET PasswordHash = 'password123',
    FailedLoginAttempts = 0,
    IsLocked = 0
WHERE Username IN ('renz.arriola', 'rene.jay', 'kyle.bautista');
```

**This resets ALL 5 accounts to plaintext.** Then all accounts are consistent.

## Then: rehash all of them via the existing endpoint

With the API running:

```text
POST http://localhost:5035/api/tenant/1/dev/rehash-credentials
```

That endpoint reads every credential whose `PasswordHash` doesn't look like a BCrypt hash (i.e. doesn't start with `$2a$` and isn't 60 chars) and hashes it. Since we just reset them to `password123` plaintext, all 5 get hashed properly with a fresh salt from BCrypt.

**Response should be:**

```json
{
  "message": "Rehash complete.",
  "updated": 5,
  "skipped": 0,
  "total": 5
}
```

## Why the hardcoded hash failed

The hash `$2a$11$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy` is a well-known test hash — but it's for `"password"`, not `"password123"`. I misremembered. That's on me.

**The correct approach** is what the rehash endpoint does: generate a fresh BCrypt hash of the exact string `password123` using the same library your login endpoint verifies with. Same BCrypt version, same work factor — guaranteed to match.

## The accounts are currently locked — here's why that matters

Your login endpoint locks an account after 5 failed attempts:

```csharp
credential.FailedLoginAttempts++;
if (credential.FailedLoginAttempts >= 5)
    credential.IsLocked = true;
```

That's the correct security behavior. But it means during testing, it's easy to lock yourself out. The UPDATE above resets that.

**For future testing**, if you hit the lock again:

```sql
UPDATE Credentials SET IsLocked = 0, FailedLoginAttempts = 0 WHERE Username = 'xyz';
```

Or just re-run the reset UPDATE above for all accounts.

## Verify

After resetting to plaintext + hitting the rehash endpoint:

```sql
SELECT Username, LEFT(PasswordHash, 10) AS Prefix, LEN(PasswordHash) AS Len, IsLocked, FailedLoginAttempts
FROM Credentials
ORDER BY Username;
```

Should show:

```text
ana.barista     $2a$11$...    60    0    0
kyle.bautista   $2a$11$...    60    0    0
marco.manager   $2a$11$...    60    0    0
rene.jay        $2a$11$...    60    0    0
renz.arriola    $2a$11$...    60    0    0
```

All `$2a$11$`, 60 chars, not locked, 0 failed attempts.

Then log in as any of them with `password123`. Should work.

## One caution

**Don't hardcode a BCrypt hash in seed SQL again.** The reason: BCrypt hashes include a random salt, so a hash generated on my machine won't be identical to one generated on yours — they're mathematically equivalent for verification purposes only if they use the same work factor and BCrypt implementation. The safe pattern is: seed plaintext → run the rehash endpoint → get real hashes.

For future seed scripts, follow this pattern. If you ever need to seed an account in a fresh DB, seed plaintext `password123` and run the rehash endpoint once.

**Apply the two UPDATEs, hit the rehash endpoint, verify the hashes, then try logging in again.** Report back.

Two distinct things. Let me be precise about both.

## 1. Closing `FrmMain` should exit the app, not return to login

Right now `Program.cs` loops — so closing `FrmMain` re-shows `FrmLogin`. That's wrong for the "close the window" case.

The behavior you want is:

- **Logout button** → back to `FrmLogin` (so you can log in as a different role).
- **Closing the window** (X button, Alt+F4) → exit the app entirely.

**These need to be different signals.** The simplest way: use a flag or a distinct `DialogResult`.

### The pattern

`FrmMain`'s `LogoutBtn_Click` calls `Close()`. When the user clicks X, `FormClosing` fires and then `Close()` runs. So both paths look identical to `Program.cs`.

**Fix:** add a flag on `FrmMain` that indicates "closed via logout" vs "closed via X."

**In `FrmMain.cs`:**

Add a field:

```csharp
public bool ClosedViaLogout { get; private set; }
```

In `LogoutBtn_Click`, before `Close()`:

```csharp
ClosedViaLogout = true;
EmployeeSession.End();
Close();
```

**In `Program.cs`, the loop changes:**

```csharp
while (true)
{
    using var login = new FrmLogin();
    if (login.ShowDialog() != DialogResult.OK)
        return;   // user closed login — exit

    var main = new FrmMain();
    Application.Run(main);

    // If the user closed FrmMain via the X button, exit the app.
    // If they clicked Logout, loop back to the login screen.
    if (!main.ClosedViaLogout)
        return;
}
```

**Result:**

- Click X on `FrmMain` → app exits.
- Click Logout on `FrmMain` → back to `FrmLogin`.

## 2. Confirmation on close

You said "closing the UI should have a confirmation? i think?"

**Two interpretations:**

**A. Confirm before exiting the whole app.** When the user clicks X on `FrmMain`, show "Are you sure you want to exit? Any in-progress sale will be lost." Then either exit or stay.

**B. Confirm before logging out** (which already happens — the existing `LogoutBtn_Click` shows a confirm dialog). If that's already in place, no change needed.

**My read:** you want **(A)** — a confirmation on window close. That's reasonable for a POS because of the in-progress sale risk. If a Barista has 3 drinks in the cart and accidentally hits X, they lose the sale.

**Fix:** override `FormClosing` in `FrmMain`:

```csharp
protected override void OnFormClosing(FormClosingEventArgs e)
{
    base.OnFormClosing(e);

    // Only confirm on user-initiated closes (X button, Alt+F4) — not on programmatic
    // Close() from Logout, which sets ClosedViaLogout first.
    if (e.CloseReason == CloseReason.UserClosing && !ClosedViaLogout)
    {
        var confirm = MessageBox.Show(this,
            "Are you sure you want to exit? Any in-progress sale will be lost.",
            "Exit Morcaffein",
            MessageBoxButtons.YesNo,
            MessageBoxIcon.Question);

        if (confirm != DialogResult.Yes)
        {
            e.Cancel = true;
            return;
        }
    }
}
```

**What this does:**

- Closing via X or Alt+F4 → confirm dialog → if No, the window stays open. If Yes, the app closes.
- Logout → no confirmation prompt here (the logout handler already has its own confirm). After logout, `Close()` runs; the `ClosedViaLogout` flag suppresses the exit confirmation.

## 3. The API process staying alive after the UI closes

This one's trickier. **When you run from Visual Studio in Debug mode, the API is a separate process.** Closing the WinForms app doesn't automatically kill the API — VS keeps it running because it's a separate debug session.

**Three ways to handle this:**

**A. Handle it manually.** Just stop the API in VS when you're done. This is what most people do during development. The API staying up is actually *convenient* — you don't have to restart it every time you close the UI to test something.

**B. Have the WinForms app send a "shutdown" call to the API on exit.** Then the API has a `POST /dev/shutdown` endpoint that kills its own process. **Not recommended** — it's fragile, and if the API is ever hosted centrally (which it will be in production), letting any client kill it is a security hole.

**C. Bundle the API and WinForms app into one process.** Way too much work for a college project.

**My strong recommendation: A.** Leave the API running.

**Why this is actually correct:**

In real deployment, the API runs on a server. It doesn't shut down when any client closes. The fact that during development it lives on your laptop and stays running is exactly how the real thing works — it's *not* a bug. The API is meant to be always-up.

You can stop it manually when you're done for the day. Or set up multi-project startup in VS, which launches both, and stopping the debug session (the red square) stops both at once.

**If you're not using multi-project startup:**
Right-click the solution → **Configure Startup Projects** → **Multiple startup projects** → set both `CRM_Morcaffein.api` and `CRM_Morcaffein.winforms` to **Start**. Now F5 launches both, and Shift+F5 (stop debugging) stops both.

That's the fix — not a code change, just VS configuration.

```csharp
using CRM_Morcaffein.Session;
using CRM_Morcaffein.Theme;
using CRM_Morcaffein.winforms.Views.Controls;

namespace CRM_Morcaffein.winforms.Views
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Staff console shell: a right-docked nav strip and a content area that swaps in
    /// whichever tab is active. The nav items shown depend on the logged-in employee's
    /// role:
    ///   Barista → Transactions, Customers, Feedback
    ///   Manager → Dashboard, Campaign, Customers, Feedback
    ///   Admin   → Dashboard, Approvals, Manage Users
    ///
    /// Customers and Feedback reuse the same views across roles that have them.
    /// Placeholder tabs (Dashboard, Campaign, Approvals, Manage Users) use PlaceholderView.
    /// </summary>
    public partial class FrmMain : Form
    {
        /// <summary>
        /// Set to true when the user clicks Log Out. Used by Program.cs to decide whether
        /// to loop back to the login screen (logout) or exit the app (X button).
        /// </summary>
        public bool ClosedViaLogout { get; private set; }

        public FrmMain()
        {
            InitializeComponent();

            // Login already seeded EmployeeSession before this form was launched.
            var employee = EmployeeSession.Current!.Employee;
            staffNameLabel.Text = employee.FullName;
            staffRoleLabel.Text = employee.Role;
            avatarPanel.Paint += AvatarPanel_Paint;
            brandMarkPanel.Paint += BrandMarkPanel_Paint;

            BuildNavButtons(employee.Role);

            logoutBtn.Click += LogoutBtn_Click;
        }

        private void FrmMain_Load(object sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            // Activate the first nav button that was built for this role.
            if (sidebarPanel.Controls.OfType<Button>().Any())
            {
                var firstNav = sidebarPanel.Controls.OfType<Button>().First();
                firstNav.PerformClick();
            }
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Confirms on user-initiated closes (X button, Alt+F4). Programmatic closes
        /// (Logout) skip the confirmation because ClosedViaLogout is already true.
        /// </summary>
        protected override void OnFormClosing(FormClosingEventArgs e)
        {
            base.OnFormClosing(e);

            if (e.CloseReason == CloseReason.UserClosing && !ClosedViaLogout)
            {
                var confirm = MessageBox.Show(this,
                    "Are you sure you want to exit? Any in-progress sale will be lost.",
                    "Exit Morcaffein",
                    MessageBoxButtons.YesNo,
                    MessageBoxIcon.Question);

                if (confirm != DialogResult.Yes)
                {
                    e.Cancel = true;
                    return;
                }
            }
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Builds the sidebar nav buttons based on the employee's role.
        /// </summary>
        private void BuildNavButtons(string role)
        {
            var isManager = role.Equals("Manager", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                            role.Equals("Admin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                            role.Equals("SuperAdmin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
            var isAdmin = role.Equals("Admin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                          role.Equals("SuperAdmin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

            var navItems = new List<(string Text, Action onClick)>();

            if (isAdmin)
            {
                navItems.Add(("Dashboard", () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Dashboard",
                    "Business intelligence and reports. Coming soon."))));
                navItems.Add(("Approvals", () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Approvals",
                    "Review and approve Manager actions — point adjustments, customer edits, campaign creations. Coming soon."))));
                navItems.Add(("Manage Users", () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Manage Users",
                    "Create, edit, and deactivate employee accounts. Coming soon."))));
            }
            else if (isManager)
            {
                navItems.Add(("Dashboard", () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Dashboard",
                    "Business intelligence and reports. Coming soon."))));
                navItems.Add(("Campaign", () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Campaign",
                    "Create and manage campaigns, activate promos, send SMS notifications. Coming soon."))));
                navItems.Add(("Customers", () => ShowView(new CustomerManagementView())));
                navItems.Add(("Feedback", () => ShowView(new FeedbackManagementView())));
            }
            else
            {
                // Barista (default)
                navItems.Add(("Transactions", () => ShowView(new TransactionView())));
                navItems.Add(("Customers", () => ShowView(new CustomerManagementView())));
                navItems.Add(("Feedback", () => ShowView(new FeedbackManagementView())));
            }

            // Build the buttons. Layout from top of sidebar, stacked vertically.
            int y = 20;
            const int buttonWidth = 184;
            const int buttonHeight = 46;
            const int gap = 12;

            foreach (var (text, onClick) in navItems)
            {
                var btn = new Button
                {
                    Text = text,
                    Size = new Size(buttonWidth, buttonHeight),
                    Location = new Point(18, y),
                };
                StyleNavButton(btn, active: false);

                var capturedText = text;
                var capturedOnClick = onClick;
                btn.Click += (s, e) =>
                {
                    SetActiveNav(btn);
                    topBarTabLabel.Text = "/ " + capturedText;
                    capturedOnClick();
                };

                sidebarPanel.Controls.Add(btn);
                y += buttonHeight + gap;
            }
        }

        private void ShowView(UserControl view)
        {
            contentPanel.Controls.Clear();
            view.Dock = DockStyle.Fill;
            contentPanel.Controls.Add(view);
        }

        private void SetActiveNav(Button active)
        {
            foreach (var button in sidebarPanel.Controls.OfType<Button>())
            {
                button.BackColor = button == active ? BrandPalette.NavActiveBackground : BrandPalette.NavBackground;
                button.ForeColor = button == active ? BrandPalette.NavActiveText : BrandPalette.NavText;
                button.Font = button == active ? BrandPalette.BrandFontBold(10f) : BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(10f);
            }
        }

        private void LogoutBtn_Click(object? sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            var confirm = MessageBox.Show(this,
                $"Log out of {EmployeeSession.Current?.DisplayName}'s session?",
                "Log Out", MessageBoxButtons.YesNo, MessageBoxIcon.Question);

            if (confirm != DialogResult.Yes)
                return;

            ClosedViaLogout = true;
            EmployeeSession.End();
            Close();
        }

        private void BrandMarkPanel_Paint(object? sender, PaintEventArgs e)
        {
            var g = e.Graphics;
            g.SmoothingMode = System.Drawing.Drawing2D.SmoothingMode.AntiAlias;

            using var brush = new SolidBrush(BrandPalette.Brand);
            g.FillEllipse(brush, 0, 0, brandMarkPanel.Width - 1, brandMarkPanel.Height - 1);

            using var font = BrandPalette.BrandFontBold(11f);
            var textSize = g.MeasureString("M", font);
            g.DrawString("M", font, Brushes.White,
                (brandMarkPanel.Width - textSize.Width) / 2, (brandMarkPanel.Height - textSize.Height) / 2);
        }

        private void AvatarPanel_Paint(object? sender, PaintEventArgs e)
        {
            var g = e.Graphics;
            g.SmoothingMode = System.Drawing.Drawing2D.SmoothingMode.AntiAlias;

            using var brush = new SolidBrush(BrandPalette.Brand);
            g.FillEllipse(brush, 0, 0, avatarPanel.Width - 1, avatarPanel.Height - 1);

            var initials = GetInitials(EmployeeSession.Current?.DisplayName);
            using var font = BrandPalette.BrandFontBold(11f);
            var textSize = g.MeasureString(initials, font);
            g.DrawString(initials, font, Brushes.White,
                (avatarPanel.Width - textSize.Width) / 2, (avatarPanel.Height - textSize.Height) / 2);
        }

        private static string GetInitials(string? fullName)
        {
            if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(fullName))
                return "?";

            var parts = fullName.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);
            return parts.Length switch
            {
                0 => "?",
                1 => parts[0][..1].ToUpperInvariant(),
                _ => (parts[0][..1] + parts[^1][..1]).ToUpperInvariant(),
            };
        }

        private static void StyleNavButton(Button button, bool active)
        {
            button.FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat;
            button.FlatAppearance.BorderSize = 0;
            button.TextAlign = ContentAlignment.MiddleLeft;
            button.Padding = new Padding(16, 0, 0, 0);
            button.Font = active ? BrandPalette.BrandFontBold(10f) : BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(10f);
            button.Cursor = Cursors.Hand;
            button.BackColor = active ? BrandPalette.NavActiveBackground : BrandPalette.NavBackground;
            button.ForeColor = active ? BrandPalette.NavActiveText : BrandPalette.NavText;
            button.FlatAppearance.MouseOverBackColor = BrandPalette.NavHoverBackground;
        }
    }
}
```

You also need to update `Program.cs` to check `ClosedViaLogout`. Replace it with:

```csharp
using CRM_Morcaffein.winforms.Services.Api;
using CRM_Morcaffein.winforms.Views;

namespace CRM_Morcaffein
{
    internal static class Program
    {
        [STAThread]
        static void Main()
        {
            ApplicationConfiguration.Initialize();

            // Prewarm the API (fire-and-forget).
            _ = Task.Run(async () =>
            {
                try
                {
                    using var http = new HttpClient
                    {
                        BaseAddress = new Uri(ApiConfig.BaseUrl),
                        Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10),
                    };
                    await http.GetAsync($"api/tenant/{ApiConfig.CompanyId}/customers?page=1&pageSize=1");
                }
                catch { }
            });

            // Loop: login → main → (if logout) login again. If the user closes the main
            // window with the X button, exit the app.
            while (true)
            {
                using var login = new FrmLogin();
                if (login.ShowDialog() != DialogResult.OK)
                    return;   // user closed login — exit

                var main = new FrmMain();
                Application.Run(main);

                if (!main.ClosedViaLogout)
                    return;   // closed via X — exit the app
            }
        }
    }
}
```

- **Manage Users** — list Employees, create new (name, contact, email, role, username, password), edit, deactivate. Backed by new `IEmployeeService` + `EmployeeApi` + `EmployeesController` on the API.
- **Approvals** — a queue of Manager-initiated actions to review. Three sub-queues: point adjustments, customer edits, campaign creations. The API already has points-adjustment approve/reject; customer edits and campaign approvals need endpoints.
- **Dashboard (read-only)** — visible to Admin, no export.

**2. Manager UI (real)**

- **Dashboard** — same content as Admin's, but with an "Export to PDF" button.
- **Campaign** — create new campaigns (blocked until Admin approves), edit existing ones, activate/deactivate, send SMS (once + one resend).
- **Approve staff point adjustments** — the existing request-side UI already exists in the Customer drawer; the approve/reject half becomes reachable because the session is a Manager.
- **Resolve/dismiss feedback** — was removed from the Staff app; it comes back on the Manager side.
- **Customer editing** — applies immediately, queues for Admin review.
- **Feedback resolution** — direct Manager action, no Admin review.

**3. Dashboard / Business Intelligence (its own workstream)**

- Content: sales over date range, top-selling drinks, top customers, feedback summary, points issued vs redeemed.
- PDF export (QuestPDF or similar).
- Shared view for Manager and Admin, export button only for Manager.

**4. SMS/Email**

- Interface + stub provider (logs to file).
- Triggers: campaign activation (broadcast to all customers), account creation (welcome message), near-tier points (within 20 points of upgrade).
- Real provider deferred.

## The dependency graph

- **Dashboard** is a dependency of both Admin UI and Manager UI. So it might be smart to **build Dashboard first**, then both Admin and Manager UIs can just embed it.
- **Approvals** depends on the Manager-side actions existing to be approvable. If Manager can't create a campaign yet, there's nothing to approve. So it makes sense to build **Manager actions first, then Admin approvals**.
- **Manage Users** is independent — doesn't depend on anything else. Could be first.

## My proposed order

**Option A — Admin first (per your earlier preference):**

1. **Manage Users** (Admin) — independent, foundational.
2. **Admin Dashboard (read-only)** — builds the Dashboard view, gets it working.
3. **Approvals (Admin)** — but this waits on Manager actions existing.
4. **Manager Campaign** — creates campaigns to be approved.
5. **Manager Customer editing** — applies immediately, queues for Admin.
6. **Manager Feedback resolution** — direct.
7. **Manager Dashboard with PDF export** — reuses the Dashboard view from step 2.
8. **SMS/Email**.
9. **SuperAdmin x Admin** (deferred).

**Option B — Manager first:**

1. **Manager Dashboard with PDF export** — builds the Dashboard view.
2. **Manager Campaign** — create/manage campaigns.
3. **Manager Customer editing**.
4. **Manager Feedback resolution**.
5. **Manage Users** (Admin) — independent.
6. **Admin Dashboard (read-only)** — reuses Dashboard from step 1.
7. **Admin Approvals** — now has Manager actions to review.
8. **SMS/Email**.
9. **SuperAdmin x Admin** (deferred).

**My honest recommendation: Option B.** Reasons:

- Manager actions *produce* the things Admin approves. Building Manager first means when you build Approvals, you have real things to approve.
- Dashboard is shared; building it once and reusing it in both roles is cleaner if you start with the "primary" consumer (Manager, since Manager gets the richer version with export).
- Manage Users is independent — but it's also the least interesting/riskiest-to-build. Better to tackle the harder feature (Campaign management) while you have energy.

**But you said earlier "we're starting with admin right"** — so if you want Option A, that's fine too. The sequencing just means Approvals is built *before* there's anything to approve, and you'll test it with manually-inserted rows.

- Minimal: create + view.
- My recommendation: **create + view first**, edit/deactivate later. Simpler scope, and the essential flows work.

**5. Campaign management — what's the exact feature set?**

**7. Customer editing — full form or inline?**

## Icon sizes for your app

Three categories of icons, different recommended sizes:

### 1. Sidebar nav icons (the biggest set)

Look at your current nav buttons: **46px tall, 184px wide**. Icons sit to the left of the text, and the button has `Padding = new Padding(16, 0, 0, 0)` — so there's already 16px of left inset before the text starts.

**Recommended icon size: 20×20 or 24×24 pixels.**

- **20×20** if you want the icon to feel modest and secondary to the text.
- **24×24** if you want it to be prominent (this is more common in modern app sidebars).

I'd go with **24×24**. Reasoning: the nav text is 10pt (~13px tall glyph height), and 24px icons sit visually balanced next to that — big enough to read, small enough to not dominate.

**Hitbox considerations:** the button is 46px tall, so a 24px icon leaves ~11px top/bottom. That's comfortable.

### 2. Top-bar brand mark

Currently: **32×32 panel** painted with a brown circle and a white "M".

**Recommended: 32×32**. Already correct. If you want to replace the painted circle with an actual icon image, export at 32×32 (or 64×64 for HiDPI, downscaled in code).

### 3. Sidebar avatar (footer)

Currently: **40×40 panel** painted with a brown circle and the user's initials.

**Recommended: 40×40**. Already correct.

### 4. App icon (taskbar, title bar, Alt+Tab)

**Recommended: multi-resolution `.ico` file.** Windows wants:

- **16×16** — Alt+Tab, small window title bar
- **32×32** — taskbar, medium icons
- **48×48** — medium icons in File Explorer
- **64×64** — large icons
- **128×128** — extra-large icons
- **256×256** — thumbnails, high-DPI taskbar

You don't make six separate files — you make one `.ico` file that contains all six sizes embedded. Tools like **IcoFX**, **GIMP** (with the ICO plugin), or **[icoconvert.com](https://icoconvert.com/)** will combine them.

**Design at 256×256** (the largest size) and let the export tool downscale. If you design at 32×32 and try to upscale, it'll look blurry.

## Design conventions worth deciding now

**Style:** flat or line-based? The rest of your app is fairly flat (solid fills, no gradients, no shadows). **I'd recommend flat, monochrome.** The theme is one brand color (brown #572400) plus neutrals. If icons are monochrome, they inherit whatever ForeColor the button has — so active (dark brand color) vs inactive (muted text) states come free.

**Two approaches for tinting:**

- **A. Monochrome icons with transparency.** Design them in white or black at 24×24 with transparent backgrounds. In code, load them and use a tinting trick (or just design two variants: one light, one dark, swap based on active state). Simpler: one icon file, code recolors it.
- **B. Full-color icons.** Design them in brand brown. They won't adapt to active/inactive states, so you'd need two variants. More design work, less code flexibility.

**I'd recommend A.** Monochrome + code tinting. It's what modern app sidebars do (VS Code, Discord, Slack), and it means your icons stay on-theme even if the palette ever changes.

**Format:** PNG with alpha, or SVG if you'll render at multiple sizes. WinForms doesn't natively render SVG — you'd need a library like `Svg.NET` or `SvgRender`. **Recommendation: export to PNG at 24×24 (and 48×48 for HiDPI), transparent background.**

## What "16x16" and "48x48" are for

**Windows app icons work like this:**

- **`.ico` file** — a container that holds multiple sizes (16, 32, 48, 64, 128, 256) in one file. Windows picks the right one for the context.
- **Individual PNGs** — not directly usable as the app icon. You'd need to combine them into a `.ico` first.

**Two paths:**

**A. You provide a `.ico` file.** Best. Set `<ApplicationIcon>Resources\Branding\app.ico</ApplicationIcon>` in the `.csproj`. Windows handles everything.

**B. You provide PNGs and I convert at build time.** More complex — would need a build step or a one-time conversion. Not ideal.

**C. You provide a single PNG and I convert once, manually.** Easiest for you: give me one PNG at 256×256, I'll run it through a conversion tool locally and hand you back an `.ico` file. Then you drop the `.ico` into the project.

**My recommendation: C.** Send me the 256×256 (or larger) version of the logo. I'll produce an `.ico` with all six sizes embedded.

**If you only have 16×16 and 48×48 PNGs** (which is what the screenshot suggests), that's a problem — 16×16 is too small to upscale to 256. **Do you have a bigger source?** If not, we either use a placeholder or you re-export at a larger size.

## One problem: single .ico for the app

The `.csproj` `<ApplicationIcon>` requires **one `.ico` file** — not two. So we need a combined `.ico` that embeds both 16×16 and 48×48.

You have them as two separate `.ico` files. So:

**Options:**

**A. Combine `sixteeen.ico` + `fourtyeeight.ico` into one `app.ico` that contains both sizes.** This is the correct approach. Can be done with a free tool like IcoFX or an online combiner.

**B. Only use the 48×48 ICO.** Windows will upscale/downscale as needed. Works, but small sizes (taskbar tooltip, Alt+Tab) will be slightly blurry from downscaling.

**C. Use `twofivesix.png` to generate a proper multi-res `.ico`** (16, 32, 48, 64, 128, 256). Best quality. One file.

**My recommendation: C.** You already have the 256 source. It's a single tool run. The result is a proper `.ico` that covers all Windows contexts.

**If you want me to walk you through C:**

1. Go to **[icoconvert.com](https://icoconvert.com/)** (or any free PNG → ICO converter).
2. Upload `twofivesix.png`.
3. Select "generate multiple sizes" and tick: 16, 32, 48, 64, 128, 256.
4. Download the resulting `.ico`.
5. Save it to `Resources/Branding/app.ico`.

Then the `.csproj` gets:

```xml
<ApplicationIcon>Resources\Branding\app.ico</ApplicationIcon>
```

**But** — you said branding is your least priority. If C feels like too much work, **B is fine.** Just point `<ApplicationIcon>` at `fourtyeeight.ico`. It works, it just won't be pixel-perfect at tiny sizes. Nobody grading a college project is going to notice.

**Which do you want: B (use the 48 ico) or C (generate a proper multi-res ico from the 256)?**

If you haven't already set this, the app will fail to find the images at runtime. **Check that now** — right-click each folder in Solution Explorer → Properties → set copy behavior for all files in it.

```csharp
using CRM_Morcaffein.Session;
using CRM_Morcaffein.Theme;
using CRM_Morcaffein.winforms.Views.Controls;

namespace CRM_Morcaffein.winforms.Views
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Staff console shell: a right-docked nav strip and a content area that swaps in
    /// whichever tab is active. The nav items shown depend on the logged-in employee's
    /// role:
    ///   Barista → Transactions, Customers, Feedback
    ///   Manager → Dashboard, Campaign, Customers, Feedback
    ///   Admin   → Dashboard, Approvals, Manage Users
    ///
    /// Customers and Feedback reuse the same views across roles that have them.

    {
        public bool ClosedViaLogout { get; private set; }

        private const string BrandingFolder = "Resources/Branding";

            staffNameLabel.Text = employee.FullName;
            staffRoleLabel.Text = employee.Role;
            avatarPanel.Paint += AvatarPanel_Paint;

            // Top bar brand mark — load the icon PNG into the panel as a background.
            LoadBrandMarkInto(topBarBrandMarkPanel);

            BuildNavButtons(employee.Role);

                firstNav.PerformClick();
            }

        protected override void OnFormClosing(FormClosingEventArgs e)

            base.OnFormClosing(e);

            if (e.CloseReason == CloseReason.UserClosing && !ClosedViaLogout)

                    "Exit Morcaffein",
                    MessageBoxButtons.YesNo,
                    MessageBoxIcon.Question);

                if (confirm != DialogResult.Yes)
                {
                    e.Cancel = true;
                    return;
                }
            }
        }

        // =====================================================================
        // NAV CONSTRUCTION
        // =====================================================================

        private void BuildNavButtons(string role)
        {
            var isManager = role.Equals("Manager", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                            role.Equals("Admin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                            role.Equals("SuperAdmin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
            var isAdmin = role.Equals("Admin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||
                          role.Equals("SuperAdmin", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

            // (label, icon filename, view factory). Icon filename is the base name WITHOUT extension.
            var navItems = new List<(string Text, string IconFile, Action onClick)>();

            if (isAdmin)
            {
                navItems.Add(("Dashboard",  "Dashboard",  () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Dashboard",
                    "Business intelligence and reports. Coming soon."))));
                navItems.Add(("Approvals",  "Approvals",  () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Approvals",
                    "Review and approve Manager actions — point adjustments, customer edits, campaign creations. Coming soon."))));
                navItems.Add(("Manage Users", "User Mgmt", () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Manage Users",
                    "Create, edit, and deactivate employee accounts. Coming soon."))));
            }
            else if (isManager)
            {
                navItems.Add(("Dashboard",  "Dashboard",  () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Dashboard",
                    "Business intelligence and reports. Coming soon."))));
                navItems.Add(("Campaign",   "Campaign",   () => ShowView(new PlaceholderView(
                    "Campaign",
                    "Create and manage campaigns, activate promos, send SMS notifications. Coming soon."))));
                navItems.Add(("Customers",  "Customers",  () => ShowView(new CustomerManagementView())));
                navItems.Add(("Feedback",   "Feedback",   () => ShowView(new FeedbackManagementView())));
            }
            else
            {
                navItems.Add(("Transactions", "Cart",       () => ShowView(new TransactionView())));
                navItems.Add(("Customers",    "Customers",  () => ShowView(new CustomerManagementView())));
                navItems.Add(("Feedback",     "Feedback",   () => ShowView(new FeedbackManagementView())));

            int y = 20;

            const int buttonHeight = 46;
            const int gap = 12;

            foreach (var (text, iconFile, onClick) in navItems)

                var btn = new Button

                    Size = new Size(buttonWidth, buttonHeight),

                var capturedText = text;
                var capturedOnClick = onClick;
                btn.Click += (s, e) =>

                sidebarPanel.Controls.Add(btn);
                y += buttonHeight + gap;

        private static void StyleNavButton(Button button, bool active)
        {
            button.FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat;
            button.FlatAppearance.BorderSize = 0;
            button.TextAlign = ContentAlignment.MiddleLeft;
            // Push the text further right so the icon (drawn at ImageAlign.MiddleLeft with
            // its own padding) and the label don't collide.
            button.Padding = new Padding(46, 0, 0, 0);
            button.ImageAlign = ContentAlignment.MiddleLeft;
            // Extra 12px push for the icon itself — with Padding.Left=46 above, the icon
            // lands at ~12-14px from the left edge, text starts at ~46px.
            button.ImageBeforeText = 14;   // see note below
            button.Font = active ? BrandPalette.BrandFontBold(10f) : BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(10f);
            button.Cursor = Cursors.Hand;
            button.BackColor = active ? BrandPalette.NavActiveBackground : BrandPalette.NavBackground;
            button.ForeColor = active ? BrandPalette.NavActiveText : BrandPalette.NavText;
            button.FlatAppearance.MouseOverBackColor = BrandPalette.NavHoverBackground;
        }

        private void SetActiveNav(Button active)
        {
            foreach (var button in sidebarPanel.Controls.OfType<Button>())
            {
                button.BackColor = button == active ? BrandPalette.NavActiveBackground : BrandPalette.NavBackground;
                button.ForeColor = button == active ? BrandPalette.NavActiveText : BrandPalette.NavText;
                button.Font = button == active ? BrandPalette.BrandFontBold(10f) : BrandPalette.BrandFontRegular(10f);
            }

        // ICON / IMAGE LOADING

        private static Image? LoadIcon(string filenameWithoutExtension)
        {
            try
            {
                var path = Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, IconsFolder, filenameWithoutExtension + ".png");
                if (!File.Exists(path))
                    return null;

                // Load from bytes to avoid the GDI+ file cache and to release the file
                // handle immediately (so the file isn't locked while the app runs).
                var bytes = File.ReadAllBytes(path);
                using var ms = new MemoryStream(bytes);
                using var temp = Image.FromStream(ms);
                return new Bitmap(temp);   // full copy, no stream dependency
            }
            catch
            {
                return null;   // missing/corrupt file → no icon
            }
        }

        private static void LoadBrandMarkInto(Panel panel)
        {
            try
            {
                var path = Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, BrandingFolder, "Top Bar Icon.png");
                if (!File.Exists(path))
                    return;

                var bytes = File.ReadAllBytes(path);
                using var ms = new MemoryStream(bytes);
                using var temp = Image.FromStream(ms);
                panel.BackgroundImage = new Bitmap(temp);
                panel.BackgroundImageLayout = ImageLayout.Zoom;
            }
            catch
            {
                // Silently skip — the panel just renders empty if the brand mark isn't found.
            }
        }

        private void ShowView(UserControl view)
        {
            contentPanel.Controls.Clear();
            view.Dock = DockStyle.Fill;
            contentPanel.Controls.Add(view);
        }

        private void LogoutBtn_Click(object? sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            var confirm = MessageBox.Show(this,
                $"Log out of {EmployeeSession.Current?.DisplayName}'s session?",
                "Log Out", MessageBoxButtons.YesNo, MessageBoxIcon.Question);

            if (confirm != DialogResult.Yes)
                return;

            ClosedViaLogout = true;
            EmployeeSession.End();
            Close();
        }

        private void AvatarPanel_Paint(object? sender, PaintEventArgs e)
        {
            var g = e.Graphics;
            g.SmoothingMode = System.Drawing.Drawing2D.SmoothingMode.AntiAlias;

            using var brush = new SolidBrush(BrandPalette.Brand);
            g.FillEllipse(brush, 0, 0, avatarPanel.Width - 1, avatarPanel.Height - 1);

            var initials = GetInitials(EmployeeSession.Current?.DisplayName);
            using var font = BrandPalette.BrandFontBold(11f);
            var textSize = g.MeasureString(initials, font);
            g.DrawString(initials, font, Brushes.White,
                (avatarPanel.Width - textSize.Width) / 2, (avatarPanel.Height - textSize.Height) / 2);
        }

        private static string GetInitials(string? fullName)
        {
            if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(fullName))
                return "?";

            var parts = fullName.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);
            return parts.Length switch
            {
                0 => "?",
                1 => parts[0][..1].ToUpperInvariant(),
                _ => (parts[0][..1] + parts[^1][..1]).ToUpperInvariant(),
            };
        }
    }
}
```

**Wait — I need to flag a problem with what I just wrote.**

`button.ImageBeforeText = 14;` — that's not a real WinForms property. I invented it. **There's no built-in way to control the gap between a WinForms button's image and its text.** The `.Image` + `.TextAlign` + `.ImageAlign` combo puts them in a fixed layout that you can't easily shift.

**Also, the top bar brand panel:** in your current Designer, the field is called `brandMarkPanel`, not `topBarBrandMarkPanel`. And there's a `BrandMarkPanel_Paint` handler in the current file that I removed but which you'd still need to unhook.

```csharp
        private static Button CreateNavButton(string text, string iconFile, int width, int height)

                BackColor = BrandPalette.NavBackground,

                panel.BackgroundImage = new Bitmap(temp);
```
